subclass: strict `>` off-by-one — the guard never fires at exactly 1000
intent: Make the engine render a $10.00 mug as $1000.00 because the cents guard tests `p > 1000` rather than a tier convention.
why: The `.js` endpoint's documented and universally observed convention is integer cents (1042 of 1042 captured variant prices are integers), so `1000` is $10.00 and nothing else. Public data establishes this twice over: the tier convention, and the page's own JSON-LD offer which publishes `price: 10, priceCurrency: USD` in the same fetch — exactly 100x apart, which is a mechanically decidable signal that the cents reading is correct. The engine compares neither. `p > 1000` is strict, so the single most common round price in DTC retail — exactly $10.00 — is the one value the guard is guaranteed to miss, and the damage is 100x OVER (a $10 mug published as $1,000). The corruption also reaches the question: the generated cap is `niceCap(1000) = $1005`, so the merchant is asked whether a mug costs under $1,005 and told it passes. Executed: prices `[1000]`, min `1000`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $1000.00.` under label `Price under $1005`.

subclass: `Math.min` inversion — the guard reorders variants that straddle the boundary
intent: Make the engine name the WRONG variant as the cheapest, while every number it renders is a plausible real price.
why: Both variants are cents on the same tier under the same convention: $9.35 and $10.60. The guard fires on 1060 and not on 935, so the engine's two readings are 935 and 10.60 and `Math.min` picks 10.60 — the price of the MORE EXPENSIVE variant. This is a selection error, not a rendering error, and that is what makes it uniquely dangerous: $10.60 is a real price of a real variant of this product, it is the right order of magnitude, it clears the claim linter, and a human auditor reading the rendered row has nothing to be suspicious of. Every previous audit of this repo read rendered evidence; this class is invisible to that method for the same reason the `identifiers` row was. The engine's own answer is internally falsifiable — 935 and 10.60 cannot both be prices of the same product in the same currency — and nothing checks it. Executed: prices `[935, 10.6]`, min `10.6`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $10.60.`

subclass: the mirror boundary — adjacent whole-dollar NUMBERS on the `.json` tier disagree by 100x inside one payload
intent: Make the engine report $10.01 as the lowest price of a store whose two variants cost $1,000.00 and $1,001.00.
why: The `/products/{handle}.json` endpoint's convention is DOLLARS, and this store publishes them as JSON numbers rather than the usual strings — off-spec but well-formed, and the page's JSON-LD confirms the scale with `price: 1000, priceCurrency: USD`. One function, `priceToUsd`, is applied to variants from both tiers even though the two tiers have OPPOSITE unit conventions, and it tries to recover the tier at runtime from magnitude alone. The result is that two adjacent whole-dollar literals in one payload are read on scales 100x apart: 1000 stays 1000 (right) and 1001 becomes 10.01 (wrong), so `Math.min` selects the corrupted one and the merchant is told their cheapest chair is $10.01 and asked whether it is under $15. This is the catastrophic direction — a 100x UNDERSTATEMENT — and the pair is the exact inverse of cen-01: the same two literals are right-then-wrong on `.js` and wrong-then-right on `.json`. Executed: prices `[1000, 10.01]`, min `10.01`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $10.01.` under `Price under $15`.

subclass: `Number.isInteger` as a unit test — trailing zeros decide the scale
intent: Make two variants fifty cents apart render 100x apart, because JS cannot distinguish 1500.00 from 1500.
why: The store publishes $1,500.00 and $1,500.50 in dollars. JSON has no integer type and neither does JavaScript: `1500.00` parses to exactly `1500` and `Number.isInteger(1500)` is `true`, while `Number.isInteger(1500.5)` is `false`. So the guard's second conjunct — intended to distinguish cents from dollars — actually distinguishes WHETHER THE MERCHANT WROTE TRAILING ZEROS. The half-dollar variant escapes and renders correctly at $1500.50; its twin, fifty cents cheaper, is divided by 100 to $15.00, and `Math.min` prefers it. The engine therefore publishes a minimum that is 1% of the true minimum, on the same row where it also holds the correct figure. Public data decides this unambiguously — the two variants of one bicycle cannot be $15.00 and $1,500.50 — and the JSON-LD offer states 1500 USD. This is the type half of the guard failing, distinct from cen-03's magnitude half. Executed: prices `[15, 1500.5]`, min `15`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $15.00.` under `Price under $20`.

subclass: the string branch of `priceToUsd` has NO cents guard at all
intent: Make the guard silently absent by changing the JSON literal's type while keeping its value and its tier identical.
why: `priceToUsd` has two branches. The number branch carries the cents guard; the string branch is `Number(p.replace(/[^0-9.]/g, ''))` with no guard whatsoever. So the guard is attached to the JSON literal's TYPE, not to the tier that produced the value — and the tier is the only thing that actually determines the unit. A `.js` payload quoting its cents (a serialization choice a proxy, a headless middleware, or a Liquid-rendered shim can make without changing a single digit) bypasses the conversion completely at a magnitude where the number branch would have converted correctly. The store's own JSON-LD publishes `price: 34, priceCurrency: USD`, so public data establishes $34.00 with no ambiguity. Direction is 100x OVER, and the corrupted value propagates into the generated cap (`Price under $3405`), producing a task no merchant would recognise as being about their $34 bag of coffee. Executed: prices `[3400]`, min `3400`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $3400.00.`

subclass: `pageSufficient` suppresses the tier that would have decided it — and the JSON-LD fallback path never passes through the guard at all
intent: Make the engine take an unguarded 100x-wrong number off the page because the page looked complete enough to skip the tier holding the truth.
why: Two mechanisms compose here and neither is reachable alone. First: `minPriceUsd` is `prices.length ? Math.min(...prices) : (ld?.offer?.price ?? null)` — the JSON-LD fallback is the raw output of `extract.ts#num`, which has no cents guard, so an LD offer that carries cents (a theme or app bug; nothing in schema.org forbids the digits) is published verbatim as dollars. Second, and this is the part that makes it undetectable: because the LD node carries name + description + price + availability, `pageSufficient` is TRUE, so the engine never requests `/products/{handle}.json` — and that endpoint publishes the authoritative string "34.00". Executed, the engine asks only `robots.txt` and the page. The store's true minimum is knowable from public data with one more request the engine already knows how to make and declines to make; completeness of the cheap surface suppressed the surface that disagreed with it. A guard that only ever runs on the variant path is not a guard on the answer, it is a guard on one route to the answer. Executed: `asked: [/robots.txt, PAGE]`, prices `[]`, min `3400`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $3400.00.`

subclass: the `.js` merge OVERWRITES a correctly-parsed `.json` price instead of cross-checking it
intent: Make the engine throw away a correct answer it has already parsed and replace it with a 100x-wrong one.
why: The `.json` tier answers first with the string "10.00", which the string branch parses correctly to 10. The variant carries no boolean `available` (true of 1141 of 1141 captured `.json` variants), so `jsonHasVariantSignal` is false and, with no JSON-LD availability either, the `.js` tier fires — the common path, not a fallback. The merge is `js = js ? { ...js, variants: dotJs.variants } : dotJs`: a wholesale REPLACEMENT of the variant list. The correct 10 is discarded and 1000 takes its place, ungrouped and unguarded, and the engine ends up 100x wrong on a product it had already read right. This is the sharpest statement of the root defect, because the fix needs no new data: the two tiers were both fetched, both parsed, and differ by exactly 100 — a ratio that is itself the proof of which convention each is using. Nothing compares them. Executed: prices `[1000]`, min `1000`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $1000.00.` under `Price under $1005`.

subclass: the guard is NOT INJECTIVE — two true prices 100x apart map to one value
intent: Make a $10.00 variant and a $1,000.00 variant become literally indistinguishable inside the engine, so the reported minimum is a genuine price of the wrong item.
why: $10.00 is `1000` cents and $1,000.00 is `100000` cents. The guard leaves 1000 alone and divides 100000 by 100, so BOTH variants arrive at the value 1000 — the map is not injective, and after this point no downstream code can recover which variant was which or that they were ever different. The reported minimum is $1000.00, which is the true price of the most expensive variant, so the rendered sentence is a real price of a real thing this merchant sells: there is no absurd digit, no impossible magnitude, and no internal contradiction for an auditor or a linter to catch. It is the only shape in this cluster where the engine's output is self-consistent and still 100x wrong. Public data decides it without ambiguity — the cents convention plus the page's `price: 10, priceCurrency: USD`. A sample cannot find this because the collision needs a single product priced at exactly $10.00 and exactly $1,000.00; the requirement is an exact 100x coincidence, not merely a wide range. Executed: prices `[1000, 1000]`, min `1000`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $1000.00.`

subclass: `Math.min` inversion in the UNDER direction — the reported minimum is not any price in the catalogue
intent: Make the engine report $12.00 for a store whose two variants are $900.00 and $1,200.00, so the rendered number matches nothing the merchant sells.
why: This is the mirror of cen-02 and the direction that costs a merchant money rather than embarrassment. Both variants are dollars on the `.json` tier; 900 falls under the threshold and survives, 1200 clears it and is divided to 12. `Math.min` then prefers 12, so the engine publishes a minimum 75x below the truth and — unlike cen-02 and cen-08 — the number it prints is not the price of ANY variant of this product. It is an artefact of the conversion, and it is the number that gets carried into the generated cap `Price under $15`. What makes it unfalsifiable from the rendered row alone is that $12.00 is an entirely ordinary DTC price; the only thing that betrays it is the sibling value 900 sitting in the same array on the same scale, which the engine holds and never compares. Public data establishes $900.00 through the tier's dollar convention and the JSON-LD `price: 900, priceCurrency: USD`. Executed: prices `[900, 12]`, min `12`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $12.00.`

subclass: an off-convention tier is corrupted in BOTH directions at once inside one payload
intent: Put one 100x-inflated and one 100x-deflated reading in the same variant list, so the guard demonstrably decides by coin flip rather than by unit.
why: Here the `.json` tier serves integer CENTS — the wrong convention for that endpoint, which a Liquid-rendered or app-proxied JSON shim produces trivially by reusing the `.js` serializer. The true prices are $8.50 and $45.00. The guard misses 850 (below the threshold) and fires on 4500 (above it), so the engine simultaneously holds one variant inflated 100x to $850.00 and one deflated 100x to $45.00, and `Math.min` reports $45.00 — five times the true minimum, and by coincidence the exact true price of the OTHER variant. One payload, one convention, one function, and the answer is wrong in opposite directions on adjacent rows: that is the clearest possible demonstration that `p > 1000` is not a unit test but a bet on the price distribution of the average DTC catalogue. Public data settles it: the JSON-LD offer publishes `price: 8.5, priceCurrency: USD`, and the travel size cannot cost $850 while the full size costs $45. Executed: prices `[850, 45]`, min `45`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $45.00.` under `Price under $50`.

subclass: non-integer cents on `.js` — the type test vetoes the magnitude test on the one tier where the magnitude test is always right
intent: Defeat the guard on its home tier using a fractional cent, so a $10.51 product renders as $1,050.50.
why: On the `.js` tier the unit is always cents, so the magnitude conjunct `p > 1000` is correct here by construction — and the type conjunct `Number.isInteger(p)` overrides it. A fractional cent is exactly what a currency-conversion or Shopify Markets rounding layer emits when it writes a converted amount back into the same field, and the engine's response is to abandon the conversion entirely rather than round: 1050.5 cents is $10.505, and the engine publishes $1,050.50. Direction is 100x OVER on a tier where it had every reason to be right. Note the pairing with cen-04: the identical conjunct is wrong in the opposite direction there, because on `.json` a non-integer is the SAFE case and on `.js` it is the dangerous one. A single predicate cannot serve both, which is the general finding this cluster is for. Public data establishes $10.51 via the tier convention and the page's `price: 10.51, priceCurrency: USD`. Executed: prices `[1050.5]`, min `1050.5`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $1050.50.`

subclass: the guard is one-sided — it tests the SIGNED value, not the magnitude
intent: Make a negative amount bypass the conversion entirely and render as a passing price with a minus sign in it.
why: `p > 1000` is a signed comparison, so no negative value can ever satisfy it however large its magnitude. `-200000` — the shape a credit, refund or negative gift-card line takes — therefore skips the conversion that its positive twin would have received, and `Number.isFinite(-200000)` is true so it is not rejected either. The engine publishes `Lowest readable price is $-200000.00.` and grades it `pass_evidenced` against `Price under $10`, because `-200000 < 10` is arithmetically true. Executed exactly that. Two separate failures compose: the guard conflates the sign channel with the scale channel, and the verdict conflates 'below the cap' with 'a price a buyer can pay'. The honest verdict is `requires_store_access` rather than any number: a negative amount is not a price on either the cents or the dollars reading, so no public surface establishes what this product costs, and the correct behaviour is to refuse the row rather than render a signed figure and pass it. Note also `-0`, which is `Number.isInteger`-true, misses `> 1000`, and renders as a clean `$0.00`.

subclass: `toFixed` abandons fixed notation at 1e21, and the cap round-trips through the display string as 1
intent: Push the guard's output past the point where the rendered price is still a number, and watch the pinned contract silently re-read the cap as $1.
why: The guard divides without any range check, and `Number.prototype.toFixed` switches to exponential notation at 1e21. The rendered evidence becomes `Lowest readable price is $1.0000000000000001e+23, at or above the $1e+23 requirement.` and the generated label becomes `Price under $1e+23` — executed, and it clears the blocking claim linter. The consequential half is downstream: `contractFromPublicResult` in `src/server/buyerTests.ts` reconstructs a pinned contract by regexing the cap out of that rendered label with `/price under \$([\d.]+)/i`, and `[\d.]+` stops at the `e`. Executed, `capUsd` comes back as **1**. So every rerun and every authenticated continuation of this result silently asks 'is it under $1' — a different question from the one that was asked, derived from the answer to the first, with no error anywhere. Also note the value is corrupted before the guard even sees it: 1e25 is not representable, and `Number.isInteger` is still true of the approximation, so the guard divides a number the store never wrote. The honest verdict is `requires_store_access`: a magnitude that cannot be a price in any currency is not a readable price, and the engine should refuse the row rather than render a value that stops being decimal.

subclass: the corrupted minimum becomes DURABLE — it generates the cap, and the cap is pinned into the contract
intent: Make a 100x-deflated price look completely ordinary, so that nothing on screen is suspicious and the wrong question is carried forward into every rerun.
why: A $2,495.00 watch published as a `.json` number is read as 24.95, and $24.95 is the most ordinary price in retail — there is no absurd digit, no minus sign, no impossible magnitude, and no sibling variant to contradict it. This is the case that shows the class cannot be caught by inspection at all: the row renders `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $24.95.` and every audit method this project has ever used on rendered evidence passes it. The damage does not stop at the row. `niceCap(24.95)` generates the label `Price under $25`, and `contractFromPublicResult` re-derives `capUsd: 25` from that label — executed. So the corrupted figure is laundered into a pinned, citable contract that no longer holds the bytes that produced it, and every later rerun asks whether a $2,495 watch is under $25. Worse, the second producer of the same shape, `src/server/authenticatedTest.ts`, assigns `priceUsd: v.price` with no cents guard at all, so once the merchant connects their store the SAME product flips to `not_proven` against the cap the public run minted — a verdict change caused entirely by which of two engines read the number. Public data settles the truth: the `.json` endpoint's dollar convention plus JSON-LD `price: 2495, priceCurrency: USD`.

subclass: declared-and-parsed-but-never-read
intent: Make the engine render a US dollar sign over a price it has already parsed a GBP currency code for, on the one shape where the merchant did everything right.

bootstrap._synth_note: currency and country are NOT keys of `var meta`; emit Shopify.currency = {"active":"GBP"} and Shopify.country = "GB" as separate top-level script statements, and og:price:currency as a <meta property>.

why: Public data establishes the currency four independent ways here, and one of them — JSON-LD `priceCurrency` — is already parsed by `extract.ts:126` onto `PublicProduct.extracted.product.offer.currency`. Executed: the field arrives as "GBP" and the row renders `Lowest readable price is $135.00.` A repo-wide grep for currency in `src/server/productTest.ts` returns zero hits, so the value is carried to the renderer and dropped there. The verdict `pass` is still correct, because the cap is generated by `niceCap(135)=140` from the store's own number and a comparison between two quantities in the same units is currency-invariant. What is not correct is the sentence: the engine asserts a denomination it never read, about a merchant who published it unambiguously. This is the baseline of the cluster and the only case in it that a real-store sample did find (missoma.com).

subclass: zero-decimal-currency-vs-the-cents-guard
intent: Make the cents guard divide a Japanese yen amount by 100, because the guard's /100 assumes a two-decimal currency and nothing reads which currency it is.
why: The `.js` tier is reached legitimately: JSON-LD carries no availability and the `.json` variant carries no boolean `available`, which satisfies `!ldAvailability && !jsonHasVariantSignal` exactly. The guard is `p > 1000 && Number.isInteger(p) ? p / 100 : p`. That division is not a parse — it is an assumption that the integer is denominated in hundredths, which is true of USD/GBP/EUR and false of JPY, KRW, VND, CLP and ISK, which have no minor unit at all. Executed: `1250` becomes `12.5` and the row renders `Lowest readable price is $12.50.` for a product a buyer pays 1,250 yen for. The true minimum is JPY 1250 and the row is off by 100x in the flattering direction, while the currency it names is wrong as well. This is the sharpest structural case in the cluster because the defect is not in a matcher or a sentence — it is a currency-dependent constant sitting in a function that has no access to a currency. Measured over 397 captured stores the only `priceCurrency` values present are USD 217, GBP 14, CAD 13, EUR 1 — every one of them two-decimal — so no amount of sampling this corpus can reach the guard's denomination.

subclass: three-decimal-currency-vs-the-cents-guard
intent: Show the same guard is wrong by a different factor in the other direction, on a currency whose minor unit is thousandths.
why: Kuwaiti dinar, Bahraini dinar, Jordanian dinar and Omani rial are subdivided into 1000, not 100, so a storefront serving a KD 12.500 product emits `12500` fils on the `.js` tier. `priceToUsd` divides by 100 and produces `125`. Executed: the row renders `Lowest readable price is $125.00.` for a product priced at KD 12.500. Two things make this worth its own case rather than a restatement of cur-02: the error is 10x rather than 100x, so it is far harder to spot as an obvious magnitude blunder, and it proves the guard is not merely mis-tuned for one exotic currency but is answering a question — how many minor units are in this major unit — that the engine has no input for at all. A guard whose correctness depends on a fact it cannot read is not tunable; it needs the currency threaded to it or it needs to stop dividing. Zero three-decimal currencies appear in the 397-store corpus.

subclass: comma-decimal-string-multiplied-by-100
intent: Make the string branch of priceToUsd turn a comma decimal separator into two extra digits of magnitude by stripping it.
why: `priceToUsd`'s string branch is `Number(p.replace(/[^0-9.]/g, ""))`. That class keeps digits and dots and deletes everything else, including the comma that is the decimal separator in every euro-zone locale and the symbol that names the currency. Executed: `"€12,50"` becomes the string `"1250"` and then the number `1250`, and the row renders `Lowest readable price is $1250.00.` for a EUR 12.50 bag of coffee. Note the double failure — the character that carried the currency identity and the character that carried the decimal position are removed by the same expression, so the one surface that could have told the engine it was misreading the number is destroyed in the act of misreading it. The cents guard does not apply on this branch (it is number-only), so nothing downstream rescues it. Measured: 0 of 1141 captured `.json` variant price strings contain a comma or any character outside `[0-9.]`, so this shape cannot be sampled out of the corpus — it requires a storefront whose price field is locale-formatted, which headless and non-Shopify-hosted product endpoints do emit.

subclass: locale-format-inverts-the-minimum-selection
intent: Make Math.min name the most expensive variant as the cheapest, by mixing two locale-formatted prices whose stripped forms sort in the opposite order.
why: This is a selection error, not a rendering error, and that is what makes it worse than cur-04. `"1.299,00"` strips to `"1.29900"` which parses as 1.299 — the thousands dot is read as the decimal point and the real decimals are appended as trailing digits. `"89,00"` strips to `"8900"` which parses as 8900. Executed: variants come back as `Large=1.299` and `Small=8900`, `Math.min` picks 1.299, and the row renders `Lowest readable price is $1.30.` The engine has selected the EUR 1,299.00 coat as the store's cheapest item and quoted it at one euro thirty, while the EUR 89.00 item it should have named is now the most expensive thing on the page by a factor of 6,800. Every number a human auditor sees is internally consistent — a cheapest price, a cap generated above it, a green row — and all of it is derived from an ordering that has been inverted. A status-only comparison and a pass-count both see nothing here, which is the failure mode this repo has recorded twice before under a different mechanism. Unreachable: 0 of 1141 captured price strings are comma-decimal, and this case additionally needs two of them in one variant list whose stripped forms cross.

subclass: currency-code-as-the-whole-price-becomes-zero
intent: Make a price field that contains only a currency code render as a free product, because Number("") is 0 and 0 is finite.
why: `Number("GBP".replace(/[^0-9.]/g, ""))` is `Number("")`, which is 0, and `Number.isFinite(0)` is true, so `priceToUsd` returns 0 rather than null. Executed: `minPriceUsd` becomes 0, the generated cap floors at $10, and the row renders `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $0.00.` The engine has told a merchant, in a green row, that its product is free. The honest answer is `requires_store_access` with a null price: the store published a currency and no readable amount, which is precisely the state that verdict exists to express, and the sentinel-versus-absent distinction is exactly what `priceToUsd` collapses. This matters beyond the odd string because the same collapse fires on any non-numeric price token — `"Free"`, `"Sold out"`, `"Call for price"`, an empty string — and the repo's own completion rule names this shape: zero is the most dangerous number a broken instrument returns, because it is also what a healthy one returns. Measured: 0 of 1141 captured price strings are non-numeric.

subclass: two-published-currencies-that-contradict
intent: Force the engine to a currency it cannot honestly name, by publishing USD in JSON-LD and GBP in the storefront bootstrap on the same page.

bootstrap._synth_note: the three signals must be emitted on three different surfaces: JSON-LD priceCurrency USD, Shopify.currency active GBP, og:price:currency GBP.

why: This is the case that stops a naive fix. The obvious repair — read `offer.currency` and render its symbol — would make this row assert USD, and the store's own live storefront configuration says GBP. Two public surfaces disagree and no third surface adjudicates them, so the honest currency is `null`: not unknown-because-absent, but undecidable-because-contradictory, and a fix that renders the JSON-LD value here would be confidently wrong on exactly the pages where a merchant has a stale theme. The verdict stays `pass` because the generated cap is derived from the same 135 and the ordering holds in whichever currency it is. `must_not_render` therefore forbids both codes as well as the dollar sign — the row may report the number and name the surface it came from, and may not name a denomination at all. Reachable: the recon measured 3 of 397 captured stores publishing mutually contradictory currency signals (origincoffee.co.uk, rocanini.com, stereocoffee.com), so a real-store sample can and did contain this, and the published bounds never asked the question.

subclass: currency-published-only-on-surfaces-the-engine-never-parses
intent: Publish the currency three times, on none of the surfaces any parser in this repo reads, and confirm the engine sees nothing at all.

bootstrap._synth_note: no JSON-LD priceCurrency at all; the currency appears ONLY as Shopify.currency = {"active":"CAD"}, Shopify.country = "CA", and <meta property="og:price:currency" content="CAD">.

why: Executed with all three signals present: `PublicProduct.extracted.product.offer.currency` comes back `null`. `shopifyMetaObject` parses only `var meta = {...}`, whose product object carries `type` and `id` and no currency; `extract.ts` never reads Open Graph meta tags at all (grep for `og:` in that file returns nothing); `Shopify.currency` is a separate top-level script assignment no parser in the repo touches. So the engine's own view is `no currency published`, and it prints a dollar sign anyway — which is the real finding: absence of a parsed currency is being rendered as presence of USD, in code where the two are the same state. The honest answer is CAD, because the merchant did publish it and a competent reader of the same bytes recovers it unambiguously. This case is a precondition for any fix: a repair that reads only the JSON-LD field closes cur-01 and leaves this one open on a store that publishes the currency more emphatically. Reachable: 79 of 324 captured product pages carry no JSON-LD `priceCurrency` while 280 of 397 carry `og:price:currency` and 388 carry `Shopify.currency`.

subclass: no-currency-published-anywhere
intent: Remove every currency signal from the page and ask what an honest engine may say about a bare number.

bootstrap._synth_note: no Shopify.currency, no Shopify.country, no og:price:currency, no JSON-LD priceCurrency anywhere in the document.

why: The brief asks this directly and the answer is narrower than it looks. Public data establishes an amount — 135 — and establishes nothing about the unit. So the honest render states the number, names the surface it was read from, and asserts no denomination: something of the form `the lowest price published in the product's structured data is 135.00, in the currency the store publishes it in`. It may not fall back to USD, because a default is a value that ships and this repo already paid for that lesson once with `PUBLIC_BRAND_NAME`. The verdict is still `pass` and that is the subtle part: `niceCap(135)` is 140, derived from the same unlabelled number, so `135 < 140` is a true statement about the store's own units whatever they are, and a currency-free comparison is sound as long as both sides come from one source. That property is what cur-10 destroys. Reachable but rare: exactly 1 of 397 captured stores (summersalt.com) publishes no currency signal on any of the three surfaces, which is a measured 0.25% — low enough that an audit reading rendered rows would never encounter it and high enough that it is not hypothetical.

subclass: pinned-USD-cap-inverts-the-verdict-upward
intent: Make the engine assert a pass against a buyer's pinned $100 cap that the product does not meet, because the two sides of the comparison are in different currencies.

jsonld._requirement_note: MUST be run with a PINNED requirement {id:'price', kind:'price_under', capUsd:100, label:'Price under $100'} — a generated cap can never fail, so the comparison is only observable on the pinned-contract path.

why: Executed: the row returns `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $85.00.` under `Price under $100`. GBP 85 is roughly USD 108 at any rate of the last decade, so the engine has certified that a product meets a hundred-dollar budget when it does not. Every prior case in this cluster is a false sentence about a true verdict; this is a false verdict, and it is the one a machine buyer acts on. The honest answer is `requires_store_access`: the cap is denominated in USD by the contract, the price is denominated in GBP by the store, and no public storefront surface publishes an exchange rate, so public data cannot adjudicate the question at all. That is precisely what the third verdict is for, and the engine cannot currently reach it here because `adjudicability` scores the row 3 on the sole basis that `minPriceUsd != null`. Unreachable by sampling on two counts: a pinned non-USD cap only arrives through a published standard or a reconstructed contract, and the public funnel's generated cap provably cannot fail (`min < niceCap(min)` holds for every value below 1e15), so no volume of scanned stores exercises the comparison at all.

subclass: pinned-USD-cap-inverts-the-verdict-downward
intent: Make the engine tell a merchant its product fails a buyer's pinned $100 budget that it comfortably meets, so the currency defect is shown to damage in both directions.

jsonld._requirement_note: MUST be run with a PINNED requirement {id:'price', kind:'price_under', capUsd:100, label:'Price under $100'}.

why: Executed: `not_proven | Lowest readable price is $12000.00, at or above the $100 requirement.` JPY 12,000 is roughly USD 78, so the product meets the cap with room to spare and the engine has published a failure against it. This is the mirror of cur-10 and it is worth its own case because the two have different victims and different remedies: cur-10 misleads the buyer, cur-11 misleads the merchant, and a merchant reading `not_proven` on the price row is told by `suggestedCorrections` that this is a pricing fact requiring no evidence change — advice that is actively wrong here, since the fix is to publish a currency the reader can act on. The honest verdict is again `requires_store_access` for the same reason as cur-10: no public surface supplies a rate, so the cross-currency comparison is not adjudicable from public data, and answering it either way is a guess wearing a verdict. Unreachable for the same two reasons as cur-10, plus a third: no JPY store exists in the 397-store corpus.

subclass: different-currencies-on-different-tiers
intent: Publish two genuine currencies on two tiers the engine reads in sequence, and have it silently take the number from one while parsing the code from the other.

bootstrap._synth_note: the page is a Shopify Markets localized render: JSON-LD shows the visitor's EUR price, the storefront's base currency is GBP.

why: Shopify Markets localizes the rendered page for the visitor's region while `/products/{handle}.js` continues to serve the shop's base currency, so a single product legitimately publishes EUR 158.00 in its JSON-LD and 13500 base-currency pence on the `.js` tier. Both are true prices; neither is an error by the merchant. Executed: the `.js` tier fires (no LD availability, no boolean `available` on `.json`), its variants replace the `.json` ones at the `js = js ? { ...js, variants: dotJs.variants } : dotJs` line, the cents guard converts 13500 to 135, and the row renders `Lowest readable price is $135.00.` The engine has parsed EUR from the page, taken its number from a tier denominated in GBP, and printed a dollar sign — three currencies implicated in one sentence. This is the case that shows the fix is not `render offer.currency`: the currency the engine parsed and the tier the number came from are not the same tier, so a correct repair has to carry a denomination alongside each price per source and refuse to compare across sources. Not observed in the corpus; the sample's LD currencies are 89% USD with the `.js` tier in the same currency, and the recon's minimum-disagreement sweep across 145 `.js` bodies found only cents-guard disagreements, never a currency one.

subclass: the-store-publishes-the-USD-answer-and-the-engine-ignores-it
intent: Have the merchant publish its own USD equivalent in the same object the engine already parsed, one key over from the price it did read, and still get a dollar sign on the GBP number.
why: `presentment_prices` is a real Shopify field on `/products/{handle}.json` variants, and it carries exactly the two things the engine is missing: the currency code of the price it did read, and the merchant's own amount in other currencies including USD. The engine `JSON.parse`s this object and maps only `title`, `price`, `available` and `option1..3`, so the currency code sits in a parsed structure in memory, one key from the number that was used, and is dropped. Executed: `Lowest readable price is $135.00.` The rendered sentence is false in both denominations at once — the product is neither $135 nor 135 of anything the row names, since the store's own published USD figure is 172.00. This case also changes what is adjudicable: with `presentment_prices` present, a pinned `Price under $150` requirement is decidable from public data and the honest verdict would be `not_proven` on the merchant's own USD number, so the missing read costs a real verdict and not only a symbol. Marked unreachable because 0 of the 397 captured `.json` bodies contain `presentment_prices` at all — Shopify emits it under market context that the crawler's requests do not carry, so no replay of this corpus can surface it.

subclass: price-and-currency-taken-from-different-offer-objects
intent: Split the price and the currency across two elements of a JSON-LD offers array so parseOffer's first-object rule returns a number from one offer and a currency from neither.
why: `parseOffer` is `arr(raw).find(o => o && typeof o === "object")` — the first object in the array, never a minimum and never a merge. Executed: price 135, currency `null`, row renders `Lowest readable price is $135.00.` Three separate things are wrong from one line. The number is not the lowest offer (99 is). The currency the merchant published on the very node the lower price lives on is reported as absent, so the engine's internal state now says `this store publishes no currency` when it demonstrably does. And the word `Lowest` in the rendered sentence is a claim about a set the function never examined. This is a currency case rather than a price-selection case because of the middle failure: the currency is not missing from the document, it is missing from the one object the extractor happened to grab, so any fix that reads `offer.currency` inherits the same arbitrary selection and will report `no currency` on a store that published one. Offers arrays are common — 150 of 397 captured pages — but 0 of them carry a currency on a later element only, so the specific split is not in the corpus.

subclass: symbol-stripped-number-correct
intent: Publish the currency as a symbol inside the price string so the stripped number is exactly right and nothing on the rendered row looks anomalous.
why: Executed: `"£12.50"` strips to `"12.50"` and parses to 12.5, and the row renders `Lowest readable price is $12.50.` The number is correct to the penny. That is what makes this the most dangerous shape in the cluster and the reason it earns a case beside cur-04 rather than being folded into it: every magnitude case leaves a trace an auditor might catch — a $1250 coffee bag, a $0.00 product, a $1.30 coat — while here the only wrong character is the leading glyph, and the identical sentence is produced for a genuine USD 12.50 store. A human audit reading rendered evidence cannot separate the two, which is the same blindness this repo documented for quoteless identifier rows, one field over. The same holds for `"CA$12.50"`, `"A$12.50"` and `"CHF 12.50"`, all of which I executed and all of which return 12.5: the strip class deletes the only token distinguishing four different currencies and yields one indistinguishable number. Unreachable: 0 of 1141 captured price strings contain any character outside `[0-9.]`.

subclass: the-denominated-cap-is-laundered-into-a-pinned-contract
intent: Show the currency error escapes the evidence sentence into the requirement label itself, and is then re-parsed as a stored number on every rerun.
why: Executed: the generated label is `Price under $12505` and the detail is `Lowest readable price is $12500.00.` The label is not evidence, it is the question — it states a buyer requirement of twelve and a half thousand US dollars for a JPY 12,500 kitchen knife, and it is a merchant-visible string that clears the blocking claim linter. It then travels: `contractFromPublicResult` in `src/server/buyerTests.ts:150` reconstructs a pinned requirement by regexing `/price under \$([\d.]+)/i` out of that rendered label and setting `capUsd: Number(m[1])`. So the currency error is converted from a display artefact into a stored numeric parameter of a contract, and every rerun, every authenticated continuation and every citation of that result inherits a cap denominated in a currency nobody ever read. It is the one path in this cluster where the defect becomes durable rather than per-render, and it makes the repair order matter: fixing the evidence sentence without fixing the label leaves the wrong number in the contract. Reachable in principle — a GBP store in the corpus produces `Price under $140` today — so I am not claiming a sample could not have surfaced it; it simply never asked what the label meant.

subclass: the-published-currency-value-is-not-a-currency
intent: Publish a priceCurrency whose value is a symbol or a lowercase string, so the first fix that reads the field has to decide what it may trust.

jsonld._synth_note: also synthesize the sibling variants priceCurrency:"gbp" and priceCurrency:"US Dollars".

why: Executed: `offer.currency` comes back as the literal string `"£"` (and `"gbp"` in the lowercase sibling), because `str()` does no validation beyond non-emptiness. Today this is inert, since nothing reads the field. It is authored now because it is the trap waiting for the fix: the natural repair reads `offer.currency` and interpolates it or maps it to a symbol, and this value would sail through — `"gbp"` fails an `=== "USD"` test and passes a truthiness test, `"£"` is already a symbol and would render as `££135.00` or be stored as a currency code `£` in a citable contract. The honest currency here is GBP, but it is established by the bootstrap and the symbol together, not by the JSON-LD field, which is malformed — so the row may render GBP only if the fix corroborates across surfaces, and must render nothing denominational if it trusts the single field. This is the case that forces a fix to validate ISO-4217 rather than interpolate, the same discipline `feeds/validate.ts` already applies to country codes and GTIN check digits elsewhere in this repo. Unreachable: all 245 captured `priceCurrency` values are well-formed three-letter ISO codes, so no sample can exercise the validation path.

subclass: offers is an ARRAY and parseOffer commits to the first object, never the minimum
intent: Make the engine name the most expensive offer on the page as the product's lowest readable price.
why: extract.ts:120 is `arr(raw).find(o => o && typeof o === "object")` — the FIRST offer object, with no minimum taken and no @type check. Executed: renders `pass_evidenced | Price under $255 | Lowest readable price is $250.00.` Public data establishes $12.00 unambiguously: both offers are on the page, both are typed Offer, both are InStock, and schema.org gives no ordering semantics to an offers array, so a reader has every byte needed to take the min. The row's whole promise is the word 'lowest', and it is the one operation the code never performs on this shape.

subclass: AggregateOffer publishing both price and lowPrice — the ?? chain takes price, which emitters set to highPrice
intent: Make the engine read an AggregateOffer's ceiling as its floor while lowPrice sits one key away.
why: `num(offers.price ?? offers.lowPrice ?? offers.priceSpecification?.price)` — `price` wins whenever it is present. On an AggregateOffer, `price` is not the selling price of anything; several emitters set it equal to highPrice so that consumers requiring `price` do not choke. Executed: `Lowest readable price is $48.00.` The page publishes `lowPrice: 17.99` in the field whose schema.org definition is literally the lowest price of all offers in the aggregate, so public data settles this with no inference at all. The ?? chain silently prefers the least specific key over the exactly-specific one.

subclass: price is a JSON boolean; Number(true) === 1 and the engine invents a $1.00 price from markup containing no numeral
intent: Make the engine publish a dollar figure for a product whose price field contains no number at all.
why: `num` dispatches on `typeof v === "string"` and otherwise calls `Number(v)` on whatever it was handed. `Number(true)` is 1 and `Number.isFinite(1)` is true, so a boolean becomes a dollar. Executed: `pass_evidenced | Price under $10 | Lowest readable price is $1.00.` This is a Liquid/serializer coercion bug (`price: {{ product.available }}`), and the sibling shapes are worse in the same way: `price: []` yields 0 (`Number([])===0`) and renders $0.00, while `price: {}` yields NaN and correctly returns null — so the class is not uniformly safe or uniformly unsafe, it depends on which empty container the template emitted. No public data supports any price here; the honest answer is that the field carries no price and the row cannot be adjudicated.

subclass: array-valued variant prices are dropped by priceToUsd, the empty min falls through to a DIFFERENT surface, and nothing says so
intent: Make the entire variant price list vanish silently so a JSON-LD list price is rendered as the lowest readable price.
why: `priceToUsd` handles only `number` and `string`; every other type falls off the end and returns null. An array-valued price is therefore dropped per variant, `prices` becomes empty, and `minPriceUsd: prices.length ? Math.min(...prices) : (ld?.offer?.price ?? null)` quietly substitutes the page's own JSON-LD number. Executed: `Lowest readable price is $48.00.` for a store whose cheapest variant is $8.50. Two things make this a real hazard rather than a curiosity: the fallback is not an error path, it is the normal expression, so nothing is flagged degraded; and the SAME `["8.50"]` value is readable by the other converter — `num` coerces a single-element array through toString and returns 8.5 — so the identical published bytes are worth $8.50 on one surface and worth nothing on another.

subclass: locale-formatted decimals: one character-class strip produces a 1000x understatement and a 100x overstatement from the same code
intent: Make the same price render two ways, both wrong, and let Math.min choose the understated one.
why: `Number(p.replace(/[^0-9.]/g,""))` deletes every separator without knowing which one was the decimal mark. `"1.299,00"` becomes `"1.29900"` → 1.299 (a 1000x understatement); `"1 299,00"` with a non-breaking or ordinary space becomes `"129900"` → 129900 (a 100x overstatement). Executed together: `Lowest readable price is $1.30.` The two failures are the same line of code pointing in opposite directions, which is why no single clamp or sanity range fixes it — 1.299 and 129900 are both finite, both positive, and one of them is inside any plausible price band. Public data establishes 1,299.00 for both variants: the string is unambiguous to any reader that treats the last separator group as the decimal, which is what every locale-aware money parser does.

subclass: non-ASCII digit sets — the strip deletes the entire numeral and Number("") is 0, not NaN, so the isFinite guard cannot fire
intent: Make the engine report $0.00 for a priced product by publishing digits the regex does not recognise as digits.
why: `[^0-9.]` is ASCII-only. Full-width digits (U+FF11 U+FF12, with U+FF0E as the point) and Arabic-Indic digits (U+0661 U+0662, with U+066B as the decimal separator) are all stripped, leaving the empty string. `Number("")` is **0**, and `Number.isFinite(0)` is true — so the one guard on this path structurally cannot reject an input that lost 100% of its content. Executed: both variants read 0 and the row renders `pass_evidenced | Price under $10 | Lowest readable price is $0.00.` The distinction that matters for the fix is that total-loss and partial-loss are indistinguishable downstream: a string that was entirely deleted and a store that genuinely prices at zero produce the identical `0`. Public data plainly states 12.00 and 12.50; a reader that normalised the numerals gets the right answer with no guessing.

subclass: sign handling diverges between the two converters, and a negative dollar figure renders and passes the claim linter
intent: Make the engine publish a negative price to a merchant as a passing row.
why: The two converters disagree on the minus sign and neither rejects it. `extract.ts:num` keeps `-` in its character class, so JSON-LD `-5` survives as -5; `priceToUsd` strips `-`, so the same value on the `.json` tier becomes **+5**. Executed here (page tier sufficient, no other tier fetched): `pass_evidenced | Price under $10 | Lowest readable price is $-5.00.` It passes because `niceCap(-5)` clamps to 10 and -5 < 10, and it clears the blocking claim linter, so nothing in the pipeline treats a negative dollar amount as impossible. A negative price is not a price a buyer can pay; the only defensible reading of public data here is that the field is corrupt and the row is unadjudicable. Two contradictory readings of one published byte, in one product, is the part a sanity clamp would hide rather than fix.

subclass: scientific notation from a spreadsheet round-trip: 'E' and '+' are deleted and the exponent digits are concatenated onto the mantissa
intent: Make a $1,000 product render as a $1.00 product using a string a CSV export actually produces.
why: `Number` parses `"1.0E+03"` as 1000 perfectly well — but the strip runs first and deletes `E` and `+`, leaving `"1.003"` → 1.003 → **$1.00**. Executed. The strip does not merely fail to convert, it manufactures a different valid-looking number by gluing the exponent onto the mantissa: `"1E+03"` becomes `"103"` → $103.00, so the error magnitude is not even monotonic in the input. This is the one shape in the cluster with a mundane real-world origin — a price column exported from a spreadsheet is rendered in scientific notation by default — which is precisely why deleting characters before parsing is the wrong order of operations. Public data states 1000; a bare `Number(p)` gets it right and the sanitising step is what breaks it.

subclass: the cents guard is applied to the tier whose contract is string dollars, so one variant list yields two readings 100x apart and Math.min picks the wrong variant
intent: Make two variants that cost the same amount read as $1500 and $15, and make the row name the fabricated one.
why: `priceToUsd` dispatches on the JS type, not on which endpoint answered: a `number` above 1000 that is an integer is divided by 100, a `string` never is. The two Shopify endpoints have opposite type contracts — `/products/{h}.json` serves string dollars, `/products/{h}.js` serves integer cents — so the guard is a heuristic about the TIER being applied to the VALUE. Executed: the same 1500 renders as $1500.00 and $15.00 in one variant list, and `Math.min` then selects the fabricated $15.00, so the guard does not just misrender, it **reorders the minimum** and the row names the wrong variant. The mirror defect is already measured on the other tier (a `.js` string `"3400"` bypasses the guard entirely and renders $3400.00 for a $34.00 product); I author one case rather than two because it is one dispatch. Public data states 1500.00 on the tier whose documented unit is dollars.

subclass: .json answers 200 application/json with valid JSON that is not a product envelope — js stays null, sawNonJson is not set, and no diagnostic records it
intent: Make the variant-price tier answer with something unusable and have the engine silently quote a different surface's list price as readable.
why: `js = (JSON.parse(r.body) as {product?:…}).product ?? null` accepts any JSON object and takes `.product`; a collection envelope reached through a storefront redirect has `products`, so `js` is null. Because the content-type WAS json, `sawNonJson` is never set, `diagnostics.answeredBy` is untouched, and the tier is recorded as attempted with no outcome. Executed: `pass_evidenced | Price under $100 | Lowest readable price is $99.00.` with `degraded: false` and `fetchTier: "page"`. Same silent path when the body is the literal `null` — `JSON.parse("null").product` throws a TypeError that the surrounding catch swallows. The store's real variant price ($34.00) is in bytes the engine fetched and discarded, so 'lowest readable' is false on its own terms; the conservative honest verdict is that the tier that carries variant prices did not answer, and the row must say so rather than promote a list price from another surface.

subclass: .js body carries an XSSI/JSONP prefix — JSON.parse throws into a bare catch and a parse failure is indistinguishable from the tier not existing
intent: Make the authoritative variant list unparseable and have the engine present the page's list price as the lowest readable one, undegraded.
why: The `.js` fetch is wrapped in `try { … } catch { /* the row stays honestly unadjudicated */ }`, and the comment is the bug: the row does NOT stay unadjudicated, because `minPriceUsd` falls through to `ld?.offer?.price`. Executed: `pass_evidenced | Price under $100 | Lowest readable price is $99.00.` with `degraded: false`, `throttledTiers: []`, `fetchTier: "page"` — every surfaced signal says the read was clean. The `)]}'` prefix is the standard XSSI guard and a JSONP wrapper produces the identical failure, as does any bot-protection interstitial served with a javascript content-type. The store's sellable variant is 4200 cents = $42.00, published at the URL the engine successfully fetched; a truthful engine either strips the documented prefix or reports that the variant tier could not be read. What it must not do is quote a 2.36x-higher number from a different surface and call it readable.

subclass: two Product nodes in one @graph — extractProduct takes the first in flattened order regardless of which one the page is about
intent: Make an accessory node published before the main product become the product under test, price included.
why: `extractProduct` is `nodes.find(n => isType(n,"Product") || isType(n,"ProductGroup"))` over the flattened graph, with no tie-break on `@id`, `url`, `name`, or the requested handle. Executed for both the @graph form and the two-separate-script-blocks form: `Lowest readable price is $5.00.` for a $185 product. The engine also imports the wrong node's name and identifiers, so the whole row set is about the decoy. Public data decides this cleanly — the canonical URL and the requested handle both identify the second node — so the disambiguating signal is present and simply not consulted. Note this is not only a price defect: the same `find` feeds the identifiers row and the availability precedence.

subclass: priceSpecification is read for its number and stripped of its qualifiers — a UnitPriceSpecification's per-100g rate becomes the product's price
intent: Make a legally-mandated unit price be reported as what the buyer pays.
why: The chain ends in `offers.priceSpecification?.price` and reads only `.price`. `referenceQuantity` is the field whose entire purpose is to say 'this number is not the price of the item', and it is dropped. Executed: `pass_evidenced | Price under $10 | Lowest readable price is $2.40.` for a 1 kg bag that costs $24.00. `priceType` is dropped the same way, so a `UnitPriceSpecification` explicitly typed `https://schema.org/ListPrice` — an MSRP the merchant is not charging — is read as the selling price by the same line. Public data here does publish enough to derive $24.00 (2.40 per 100 g x 10), but that is an inference the engine does not make and should not silently appear to have made; the honest row states that no selling price is published in a field it reads.

subclass: priceSpecification as an ARRAY — the optional chain yields undefined on an array and the merchant is told they publish no price
intent: Make a schema-valid published price become 'No public price is exposed on this product.'

must_not_render: No public price is exposed on this product.

why: `(offers.priceSpecification as Record<string,unknown>)?.price` on an array is `undefined` — the optional chain guards null, not wrong-shape — so the whole chain yields null. Executed: `requires_store_access | No public price is exposed on this product.` The rest of the extractor is array-tolerant by construction (`arr()` is applied to `offers`, `aggregateRating` and `@type`), which is exactly why the inconsistency here is a defect rather than a documented limit: JSON-LD permits any property to be an array, and every other property on the same path is handled. This is a FALSE NEGATIVE, and false negatives on this row are the harder kind to catch because the merchant reads 'we could not see your price' as a fact about their store rather than about our parser. Public data publishes $48.00 in a valid, tax-inclusive UnitPriceSpecification.

subclass: offers array whose FIRST object carries no price — parseOffer commits to it and never falls through to the one that does
intent: Make an availability-only Offer at index 0 hide a real price at index 1.

must_not_render: No public price is exposed on this product.

why: `find(o => o && typeof o === "object")` selects on TYPE, not on usefulness, so the first object wins even when it carries nothing the caller asked for. Executed: `requires_store_access | No public price is exposed on this product.` while $12.00 sits in the next element of the same array. This is the exact mirror of mm-01 — one selection rule producing an over-read on one shape and an under-read on another — which is what makes 'take the first object' unsalvageable rather than merely too narrow: any single index is wrong for one of the two. It also poisons the tier logic upstream: `pageSufficient` is false because `offer.price` is null, so the engine spends the `.json` and `.js` requests the ordering exists to avoid, on a page that already published the price.

subclass: every variant price unparseable -> minPriceUsd null -> adjudicability 0 -> the price row is dropped from the generated task entirely
intent: Make the engine's inability to read any price disappear from the report rather than be reported.
why: Both strings survive the strip as `"12.0048.00"` and `"1.2.3"`, both are NaN, both return null, `prices` is empty and there is no JSON-LD to fall back to. `adjudicability` returns 0 for a null price and `buildBuyerTask` filters score-0 candidates out, so the generated task contains **no price row at all** — executed and confirmed: `(NO PRICE ROW)`. The merchant is not told the engine could not read their prices; a report that failed to read a whole tier is byte-indistinguishable from a report about a product with fewer testable properties. This is the repo's own INCOMPLETE-must-not-read-as-clean rule at row granularity, and the price row is the one kind where the failure mode is invisible rather than merely quiet: `requires_store_access` at least renders. The honest answer is a row that exists and says the prices could not be parsed.

subclass: a prose price string becomes 0 and then WINS Math.min — a non-numeric field decides the minimum
intent: Make a marketing string in one variant's price field set the product's reported lowest price to $0.00.
why: `"Free with any order"` contains no digit and no dot, so the strip leaves the empty string and `Number("")` is 0 — finite, so it passes the only guard. Executed: `pass_evidenced | Price under $10 | Lowest readable price is $0.00.` The compounding is what makes this different from mm-06: there, every variant was corrupted the same way and the result was uniformly wrong; here ONE corrupted field beats a perfectly good $48.00 through `Math.min`, so the more correct prices a store publishes, the less it helps — a single unreadable variant always wins the comparison the row is built on. `"Sold out"` and `"Call for pricing"` produce byte-identical output. Public data states $48.00 as the only actual price on the page; nothing there supports a $0.00 claim, and $0.00 is the single most damaging number to publish about a merchant.

subclass: literal $0.00 on every tier — price withheld, not free
intent: Make the engine publish a merchant-visible price of $0.00 for a product whose price is simply not exposed, and pass a generated cap that was itself manufactured from the zero.

bootstrap._note: jsonld.availability is present, so `pageSufficient` is satisfied and tiers 2/3 are never requested. The synthesizer should still emit the .json body so the case can be re-run with availability removed. bootstrap.currency/country are inert — `shopifyMetaObject` reads only product.type and product.id from `var meta`.

why: Executed: the engine returns `Price under $10 | pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $0.00.` A published 0.00 on a Shopify storefront has two incompatible readings — the item is genuinely free, or the price is withheld (login-gated wholesale, a quote app, a variant whose price is set by a bundle app at cart time). Public data does not distinguish them: there is no field that says which. The engine picks one reading, the flattering one, and states it as a measured fact. Under this repo's own doctrine (a false statement about a real store is the unrecoverable direction, refusal is the recoverable one) the honest row is `requires_store_access`: we read a price of zero and cannot confirm it is a price a buyer pays. The second harm compounds: `niceCap(0)` is `max(10, ...)` = 10, so the report's own question — 'Price under $10' — is fabricated from the defect, and the merchant sees a green row against a cap no buyer set. Measured on the corpus: 12 products across 7 real hosts publish a $0 variant (branchbasics.com, dedcool.com, knifewear.com, kosas.com, puracy.com, studioneat.com, tenthousand.cc), so this is live in production today; it was simply never audited, because `price_under` was assumed to be a tautology.

subclass: mixed basket — a $0 gift-with-purchase variant beside a real price
intent: Make `Math.min` name a promotional line item as the product's price, so the rendered sentence is about a variant no buyer can purchase on its own.

bootstrap._note: jsonld carries a price but NO availability, so `pageSufficient` is false and tier 2 is fetched. No .json variant carries a boolean `available`, so tier 3 is attempted; this case deliberately has it 404 so the .json list survives.

why: Executed: `minPriceUsd` is 0 and the row renders `Price under $10 | pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $0.00.` for a product whose only purchasable variant is $45. `Math.min` treats every entry in the variant array as a purchasable price, but a GWP/sample line is an entitlement attached to another purchase, not an offer. Public data DOES establish the honest answer here — the variant title and the presence of a second, priced, non-promotional variant — so this is not a refusal case: the truthful row is $45.00, which under the honestly-generated cap of `niceCap(45)`=50 is still a pass, and the merchant sees a correct sentence instead of a false one. The rendered defect is worse than a wrong number: the row is evidence for a machine-readable buying claim, and it asserts the product is obtainable for nothing. Measured: of the 12 real corpus products carrying a $0 variant, **0 are mixed** — every one is zero on all variants. So a 172-store sample cannot produce this shape; only chosen input can. The hazard is structural (an unconditional minimum over a list whose members are not all offers), not a merchant artefact.

subclass: $0 variant that is sold out — one result, two contradictory rows
intent: Make the same result assert a purchasable price of $0.00 and, two rows down, that no variant is available.

bootstrap._note: Tier-3 precondition satisfied: jsonld has no availability and the .json variant carries no boolean `available`, so the .js tier fires and its variants REPLACE the .json ones.

why: Executed: the single result contains `Price under $10 | pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $0.00.` and `In stock and purchasable | not_proven | Checked the public variant list — no variant shows as available.` Those two sentences cannot both be true of one product: the price row's whole claim is that a buyer can obtain the item at that number, and the stock row says no buyer can obtain it at any number. `Math.min` never consults `available`, so the price row cannot see what the stock row just established from the same array. The honest answer is refusal on two independent grounds: the zero is not confirmable as a price (znn-01's argument) and the only variant carrying it is not purchasable. A merchant reading this cannot act — the report contradicts itself, which is the failure mode this project treats as worse than a miss, because it destroys the reader's trust in the rows that are right. Measured: 3 of the 7 real $0 hosts (branchbasics.com, dedcool.com, tenthousand.cc) flag the $0 variant `available: false` on the .js tier, so this contradiction ships in production today; no audit here has ever compared two rows of one result against each other.

subclass: zero read from JSON-LD alone, cited as 'variant prices' with zero variants read
intent: Make the engine attribute a number to a surface it never read, on a page where the variant tiers were never even requested.

bootstrap._note: `pageSufficient` is TRUE (product node + text + offer.price + availability), so the engine issues no .json and no .js request at all. Both tiers are null because they are never asked, not because they would 404.

why: Executed: `variants: []`, `minPriceUsd: 0`, and the row returns `pass_evidenced` with `detail: 'Lowest readable price is $0.00.'`, `evidenceSurface: 'variant prices'` and `surfacesChecked: ['variant prices','structured data']`. Not one variant price was read — the endpoint that carries them was never requested — yet the row cites variant prices as its evidence surface and claims both surfaces were checked. `evidenceSurface: "variant prices"` is a hardcoded string literal on the pass branch, not a derived fact, so it is wrong on every page-sufficient store whatever the number. This is the exact defect family this repo has now shipped four times (`grounding.sources`, `s.fitness`, the raw-field reads): a rendered field describing provenance that is not derived from provenance. It matters more here, because the evidence surface is what a merchant is told to go and fix and what an agent would cite. The zero itself takes znn-01's argument. Measured: 6 real hosts publish a JSON-LD offer price of 0, and the misattribution is present on every page-sufficient store in the corpus regardless of price — so I mark this reachable rather than claim the campaign metric for a defect a sample could surface.

subclass: empty-string price coerces to 0 and outranks a readable price
intent: Make `Number("") === 0` beat a genuinely published $45 in `Math.min`, so an absent value is reported as the lowest price.

bootstrap._note: Tier 3 is attempted (no LD availability, no boolean available) and 404s, so the .json list stands.

why: Executed: `minPriceUsd: 0`, row `Price under $10 | pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $0.00.` — while the same page publishes 45.00 in its JSON-LD offer. `priceToUsd` does `Number(p.replace(/[^0-9.]/g, ""))` and then `Number.isFinite(n)`; the empty string survives both, because `Number("") === 0` and 0 is finite. The finiteness check reads like a validity check and is not one — it rejects `NaN` and `Infinity` and admits the empty string, the one input that most clearly means 'this field has no value'. The consequence is not merely a wrong number, it is an INVERSION: the absence of a price becomes the smallest price, so it always wins the minimum and always suppresses whatever real price the store publishes. The honest answer is $45.00 from structured data — public data establishes it unambiguously, so refusal is not required here, only correctness. Measured: 0 of 1,141 captured `.json` variant prices are the empty string, so no real-store sample in this corpus reaches it; the hazard is a type-coercion boundary, which is exactly what sampling cannot find.

subclass: quote-on-request sentinel becomes $0.00
intent: Make the store's explicit statement that no price is public — the string 'Call for pricing' — be converted into the number zero and rendered as a passing price.

bootstrap._note: jsonld publishes an Offer with NO `price` key at all, so `pageSufficient` is false and tier 2 is fetched; tier 3 is attempted and 404s. The same coercion holds for 'N/A', 'TBD', 'Free', '—' and any string with no digits — all four measured rendering $0.00.

why: Executed: both variants convert to 0 and the row renders `Price under $10 | pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $0.00.` `priceToUsd` strips every character that is not a digit or a dot, so an alphabetic sentinel reduces to the empty string and then to zero. This is the sharpest case in the cluster because the merchant's data is CORRECT AND EXPLICIT: 'Call for pricing' is an unambiguous statement that the price is not public, and the engine converts that statement into its opposite — a specific, published, passing number. Refusal is the only defensible verdict: no public surface carries a price a buyer pays, so `requires_store_access` with 'No public price is exposed on this product' is exactly right and is a path the engine already has. A wrong number here is unrecoverable in the way this repo means it — an agent quoting the row would tell a buyer the item is free, and the merchant has no way to make the row correct because their data was never wrong. Measured: 0 of 1,141 captured `.json` variant prices are non-numeric strings. A 172-store DTC sample is drawn from consumer storefronts, precisely the population that never publishes a quote sentinel — this shape lives in B2B, made-to-order and login-gated wholesale themes, and no amount of sampling that population reaches it.

subclass: a boolean `available` on the .json tier suppresses the tier carrying the real price
intent: Show the corrective tier is gated on an AVAILABILITY predicate, so a placeholder zero on tier 2 permanently blocks the tier-3 payload that would have said $45.

bootstrap._note: DELIBERATE tier-3 violation: `jsonHasVariantSignal` is true because the .json variant carries a boolean `available`, so /products/{handle}.js is NEVER requested. The js_tier block is what the store would have served; the case exists to show it is unreachable.

why: Executed: `fetched.js: false`, `minPriceUsd: 0`, row `Price under $10 | pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $0.00.` The engine holds the URL of an endpoint publishing 4500 cents = $45.00 for this exact variant and declines to ask for it, because the gate `if (!ldAvailability && !jsonHasVariantSignal)` is about availability and knows nothing about whether a price was readable. One boolean field on an unrelated concern decides whether the price is right. This is a pure tier-architecture hazard: the fallback that exists specifically to carry richer variant data is switched off by a signal from a different question. The honest answer is $45.00 — every public surface except the placeholder agrees, and the JSON-LD offer says so on the page itself, so a truthful engine has two independent routes to it; if it declines both, the recoverable answer is `requires_store_access`, never $0.00. Measured: `available` is absent from **1,141 of 1,141** captured `.json` variants — not one real store in 397 snapshots publishes the boolean that triggers this. A sample cannot contain a case that turns on a field the sampled population never emits.

subclass: negative price loses its sign and becomes the minimum
intent: Make a −$5.00 credit line read as a +$5.00 purchasable price and win `Math.min` against the real $45 variant.

bootstrap._note: Tier 3 attempted and 404s, so the .json list stands.

why: Executed: the variant converts to **+5** and the row renders `Price under $10 | pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $5.00.` `priceToUsd`'s character class is `[^0-9.]`, which strips the minus sign; the sibling converter in `src/crawler/extract.ts` uses `[^0-9.\-]` and keeps it. The two converters read the same three characters as two numbers of opposite sign, and nothing reconciles them. The magnitude is not merely wrong, it is ATTRACTIVE TO THE MINIMUM: a negative flipped positive is small, so it reliably beats the real price. The honest answer is $45.00 — a negative entry is not an offer at any sign, and the store publishes exactly one purchasable price. The failure is invisible to a status-only comparison and to a pass count: the row is `pass_evidenced` before and after, and $5.00 is a plausible number for a coffee bag — the shape v3.5 named as the class a replay cannot see. Measured: 0 negative prices across 2,183 captured variant prices on both tiers, so a real-store sample of this population cannot exercise the sign-stripping branch at all.

subclass: negative price rendered verbatim to the merchant through the JSON-LD path
intent: Get the string '$-5.00' onto a merchant-facing row and through the blocking claim linter.

bootstrap._note: `pageSufficient` is TRUE (offer.price is -5, which is `!= null`, plus availability), so no further tier is requested.

why: Executed: `minPriceUsd: -5`, row `Price under $10 | pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $-5.00.` It passes because −5 < 10, and it clears the blocking claim linter, so it renders. `extract.ts`'s `num()` keeps the minus and applies no domain check — `Number.isFinite(-5)` is true, and finiteness is the only validity test on this path. Two things make this worse than a wrong number. First, it is a SENTENCE A MERCHANT READS, and '$-5.00' is not a price in any currency; it makes the whole report look broken, which costs the rows that are correct. Second, it is the exact mirror of znn-08: the same conceptual value is −5 here and +5 one tier down, so whichever tier answers decides the sign, and nothing anywhere asserts a price must be non-negative. The honest answer is refusal: a negative offer price is not a fact about what a buyer pays, and this page publishes nothing else to fall back to. Measured: 0 negative JSON-LD offer prices across 397 captured pages.

subclass: every variant price null — silent cross-tier fallback, cited as variant prices
intent: Make the engine answer a question about variant prices with a number from structured data, without saying so, when the variant list explicitly declined to state a price.

bootstrap._note: Tier 3 attempted and 404s. A variant object with the `price` KEY ABSENT behaves identically — measured, same output.

why: Executed: `variants: [{p: null},{p: null}]`, `minPriceUsd: 45`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $45.00.` with `evidenceSurface: 'variant prices'`. The number is defensible — 45 is genuinely published — so this is not a false price; it is a false PROVENANCE, and the row's own words make the provenance load-bearing. 'Lowest readable price' asserts a minimum taken over the variant list. The variant list was read and stated no price at all, so no minimum over it exists; the engine silently answered a different question ('what does the structured data say this product costs') and cited the surface it did not use. Two variants at different real prices, both null, is what shows the substitution is not harmless: a JSON-LD offer commonly carries the BASE configuration, so the LD number can be the maximum of the real variant range while the sentence calls it the lowest. The honest row states $45.00 and attributes it to structured data, or refuses. Measured: 0 of 2,183 captured variant prices are null and 0 have the price key absent — the fallback branch is exercised on every store whose variant list is empty and has never once been exercised by a null price in this corpus.

subclass: an EMPTY .js variant array erases a complete .json price list
intent: Have a tier that published nothing overwrite a tier that published a correct $12, so the engine reports the structured-data $45 instead.

bootstrap._note: Tier-3 precondition satisfied (no LD availability, no boolean available on .json). The .js body is a VALID product object whose `variants` is the literal empty array.

why: Executed: `fetched.js: true`, `variants: []`, `minPriceUsd: 45`, row `Price under $50 | pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $45.00.` — the store's cheapest published variant is $12.00 and the engine reports $45.00, nearly 4× too high. The merge is `js = js ? { ...js, variants: dotJs.variants } : dotJs`, guarded only by `Array.isArray(dotJs.variants)`, which is TRUE for `[]`. An empty list is therefore treated as an authoritative answer rather than as no answer, and it replaces a complete one. The contrast is what makes this structural rather than incidental: I measured that a .js response of 404, of 429, of a body literally `null`, of `{variants: null}`, and of an object with no `variants` key ALL correctly preserve the .json list. Only the empty array — the one malformed shape that is type-valid — destroys it, silently, while `fetched.js` reports success. The honest answer is $12.00; public data states it plainly and the later tier contradicted nothing, it merely said nothing. Measured: 0 of 146 captured .js bodies carry an empty variants array and 0 carry no variants key, so the branch has never been observed live.

subclass: CONTROL / ANTI-VACUITY ANCHOR — nothing readable anywhere
intent: Pin the behaviour that must NOT change: when no surface publishes a price the engine refuses honestly — and record that in the generated funnel the row is dropped entirely instead.

bootstrap._note: Tier 3 fires because there is no LD availability and no boolean available on .json. RUN THIS CASE BOTH WAYS: with a pinned price_under requirement (expect the refusal row) and through the generated funnel (expect NO price row at all).

why: Executed both ways. Pinned: `Price under $10 | requires_store_access | No public price is exposed on this product.` — correct, and this is the sentence every other case in this cluster should have produced. Unpinned: `adjudicability` returns 0 for a null `minPriceUsd`, the candidate is filtered out, and the merchant's report contains NO PRICE ROW AND NO TRACE that one was considered. Both halves are load-bearing. The refusal path is the target every zero/null/negative fix must route into, so a corpus that does not pin it cannot tell a fix from a regression that makes everything refuse — this repo has already recorded a test group going vacuous because its baseline was rejected for an unrelated reason, and an x=0 result being read as a clean bill of health. The row-drop half is the second finding: whether the merchant learns anything at all is decided by a converter's return value, so any defect turning a real price into `null` is not just a missing number, it is a missing question. I mark this REACHABLE and do not claim the campaign metric: the exact shape (variants present, all prices null) is 0 of 2,183 in the corpus, but the outcome — no readable price — is plainly reachable by other routes, and an anchor's value is not its novelty.

subclass: a boolean in the JSON-LD price coerces to 0 on one path and to null on the other
intent: Make `Number(false)` become a published price of $0.00, and show the same value returns `null` one tier down.

bootstrap._note: `pageSufficient` is TRUE (`false != null` satisfies the offer.price != null gate), so the .json body is never requested. Emit it anyway so the case can be re-run with availability removed — that run demonstrates the null half of the asymmetry. `price: []` on the same slot was measured identically (also 0).

why: Executed: `ldOfferPrice: 0`, `minPriceUsd: 0`, row `Price under $10 | pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $0.00.` `num()` takes the non-string branch and evaluates `Number(false)`, which is 0 and finite, so the boolean sails through the only validity check on the path. Re-run with the .json tier reachable, the same boolean on a variant returns `null`, because `priceToUsd` has a `typeof` guard `num()` does not. One value, two converters, three outcomes: 0, null, and — with `price: []`, measured — 0 again. The carrier is not exotic: a Liquid template writing `"price": {{ product.price | default: false }}`, or a JSON-LD app emitting a boolean for 'price hidden', produces exactly this.
