Two defects stack: the value becomes a price, AND it satisfies `offer.price != null`, so it suppresses the tier that could have corrected it. The honest answer is refusal — a boolean is not a price and the page publishes nothing else. Measured: 0 boolean, array or object JSON-LD offer prices across 397 captured pages; type confusion is the definitional example of what a sample of well-formed real stores cannot reach.

subclass: a fully-structured MoneyV2 price is read as NO price
intent: Make an unambiguous, machine-readable price object produce the sentence 'No public price is exposed on this product.'

bootstrap._note: jsonld is null — the page carries a Product node with a name and description but NO offers node, so `pageSufficient` is false and tier 2 is fetched. Tier 3 is attempted and 404s. The MoneyV2 shape is what a Storefront-API-backed proxy or a Hydrogen route serving a /products/{handle}.json path emits.

must_not_render: No public price is exposed on this product.

why: Executed: every variant converts to `null` (`priceToUsd` matches neither `typeof p === 'number'` nor `'string'` and falls through to `return null`), `minPriceUsd` is `null`, and the pinned row returns `requires_store_access | No public price is exposed on this product.` That sentence is FALSE about this store: the price is exposed, in the most machine-readable form on the page, with its currency attached — the one thing the engine has never been able to read anywhere else. This is the mirror image of every other case in the cluster, and it is why the cluster is not simply 'the engine should refuse more': refusal is only the recoverable direction when the refusal is TRUE. Here the row accuses the merchant of not publishing something they published, and the suggested remedy — expose a price — is work already done. Note also that `PublicProduct` has no currency field, so even on the path where the currency is sitting in the parsed object it has nowhere to go. The honest answer is $45.00 USD. Measured: 0 of 1,141 captured `.json` variant prices are objects — every captured store serves the classic REST shape, so this is unreachable by sampling that population and becomes reachable the moment one merchant fronts their storefront with a headless proxy.

subclass: $0 price with a non-zero compare_at_price in the SAME object
intent: Show the engine renders $0.00 while the corrective number sits in the adjacent field of the very object it just parsed.

bootstrap._note: This is kosas.com's captured shape reproduced exactly: price 0 with compare_at 26.00 on tier 2 and 2600 cents on tier 3, both variants available. Tier 3 fires (no LD availability, no boolean available on .json). The `compare_at_price` key on each variant is an addition to the brief's variant shape and is the point of the case.

why: Executed against the real captured bytes: `minPriceUsd: 0`, row `Price under $10 | pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $0.00.` for a $26 product. `compare_at_price` is present, non-null and consistent across both tiers and both variants, and no code path in `fetchPublicProduct` reads it — the engine parses the object, takes `price`, and discards the field saying the item is worth 26. The mechanism generalises past this row: the corrective signal was INSIDE the parsed object, not one request away, so no fetch-budget or tier-ordering argument excuses missing it, and the same blindness applies to any future price row. The honest verdict is refusal rather than $26.00, because `compare_at_price` is a strike-through reference price and not a price a buyer pays — it establishes that 0 is not the price without establishing what the price is, which is exactly the state `requires_store_access` exists for. Measured: 4 variants on 1 real host (kosas.com) in the 397-snapshot corpus, with 1,221 variants carrying a non-null `compare_at_price` overall. Reachable, and I claim nothing else; it is authored because the mechanism — an ignored sibling field — is structural, and none of this project's five adversarial passes has ever looked at `fetchPublicProduct`.

subclass: a null in offers[0] suppresses a price published in offers[1]
intent: Make the engine assert 'No public price is exposed' about a page that exposes one, because position 0 of an offers array is empty.

bootstrap._note: The brief's jsonld slot cannot express an offers ARRAY, so `offers_shape` and `offers` are added inside it — `parseOffer` does `arr(raw).find(o => typeof o === 'object')`, i.e. the FIRST object, never a minimum. The top-level price/availability keys describe the first offer, which is what the engine will read. `pageSufficient` is false because that first price is null, so tier 2 is requested and 404s; tier 3 is suppressed because the LD availability is present.

must_not_render: No public price is exposed on this product.

why: Executed: `ldOfferPrice: null`, `minPriceUsd: null`, pinned row `requires_store_access | No public price is exposed on this product.` — about a page whose JSON-LD publishes 45.00 with an InStock offer three keys later. `parseOffer` selects the first object in the array and never revisits that choice, so a single empty leading element discards every readable price behind it. The failure is not the array selection alone (that is the offers-array cluster's territory); it is the INTERACTION WITH NULLITY — the selector has no notion of 'this offer answered nothing, try the next', because null and 'no offer' are the same state to it. Both directions of the harm are live from one mechanism: here it under-reads into a false refusal, and with a leading `price: 0` element the identical code over-reads into a false $0.00. The honest answer is $45.00, which public data establishes on the page itself with no further request. Measured: 0 of 397 captured pages have an offers array whose first element carries no price — a well-formed emitter always fills position 0, which is why only chosen input reaches this.

subclass: the .js tier's zero unconditionally overwrites a correct .json price
intent: Have tier 3 replace a correct $45.00 variant list with a zero, with no comparison of the two and no record that they disagreed.

bootstrap._note: Tier-3 precondition satisfied. The .js payload DISAGREES with the .json payload about the SAME variant — the two tiers are read at different moments and a price-rule/draft state can zero one of them.

why: Executed: `fetched.json: true`, `fetched.js: true`, `minPriceUsd: 0`, row `Price under $10 | pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $0.00.` — while the .json tier AND the JSON-LD offer both say 45.00. The merge line replaces the whole variant array with the .js one whenever it is an array; there is no reconciliation, no precedence rule stated for PRICE (the documented precedence is for AVAILABILITY), and no diagnostic recording that two tiers of one store disagreed by 45 dollars. So the last tier to answer wins, and the tier that wins is the one the engine only asks for when it is unsure about stock. This is znn-11's mechanism with the opposite payload, and together they establish the general property: the merge is a REPLACEMENT, not a merge, so tier 3 can only ever make the price worse or leave it alone — it has no path to being outvoted by two agreeing surfaces. The honest answer is $45.00, agreed by two independent public surfaces against one. Measured: all 12 real corpus products carrying a $0 variant are zero on BOTH tiers — 0 observed tier disagreements about a zero across 397 snapshots — so a real-store sample cannot separate 'the store publishes zero' from 'one tier publishes zero', which is exactly the distinction this case isolates.

subclass: shape confusion — `.json` `variants` is not an array
intent: Make the engine crash with an uncaught TypeError instead of degrading, by serving a `.json` tier whose `variants` is a JSON object keyed by index rather than an array.

jsonld.synth_note: `availability` is deliberately ABSENT so `pageSufficient` is false and tier 2 is actually requested. LD price 249 is the default (largest) variant.

json_tier.synth_note: emit `"variants":{"0":{...},"1":{...}}` — an OBJECT, not an array. The listed variants below are the members of that object.

why: Executed: `fetchPublicProduct` throws `((intermediate value) ?? []).some is not a function` at productTest.ts:1195, and the throw escapes `runProductTest` — `src/server/index.ts:664` catches it only to record a `test_failed` telemetry event and rethrow, so the merchant gets a 500. The read at :1195 is `(js?.variants ?? []).some(...)`: `?? []` only defends against null/undefined, never against a wrong TYPE, and the `.json` tier's body is assigned with a bare cast (`(JSON.parse(body) as {product?}).product ?? null`) with no shape validation anywhere. The asymmetry is the finding: the `.js` tier's identical read at :1206 IS guarded (`Array.isArray(dotJs.variants)`) and I confirmed an object-valued `.js` `variants` degrades cleanly. One tier validates the shape and the other does not. The honest verdict is `requires_store_access`: the object form is not the shape Shopify documents, so a truthful engine cannot claim to have read the variant list — but it must say that, not fall over. Ground truth is $34.00, which is under a $40 cap, so the merchant's real answer is a pass they will never see.

subclass: shape confusion — `variants` is an array of non-objects
intent: Get phantom variants into `PublicProduct` that satisfy the `readSomething` floor and the variant-count checks while carrying no price, so the price silently falls back to the JSON-LD figure.

json_tier.synth_note: emit `"variants":["Small / 34.00","Large / 58.00"]` — an array whose members are STRINGS, not objects.

why: Executed: no crash — `Array.prototype.some` exists, `"Small / 34.00".price` is `undefined`, `priceToUsd(undefined)` returns null. The result is `nVariants: 2` with `variantPrices: [null, null]`, so `prices` is empty and `minPriceUsd` falls through to `ld.offer.price` = 249. The rendered row is `not_proven | Lowest readable price is $249.00, at or above the $40 requirement.` about a store whose cheapest variant is $34.00 — the verdict itself is wrong, not just the number. Two secondary consequences, both measured: the phantom pair satisfies `readSomething` via `product.variants.length > 0`, so the engine's own last-resort floor certifies that it read something when it read nothing usable; and `product.variants` is what the `variant_option` row searches, so those rows are being adjudicated against strings. This is the same failure family as tt-01 with the crash removed, which makes it worse — nothing anywhere signals that the tier was misread. `requires_store_access` is the honest verdict for the same reason as tt-01.

subclass: byte-level encoding — UTF-8 BOM ahead of the JSON
intent: Delete the entire variant price list with three bytes the merchant cannot see, and have the engine publish the JSON-LD default-variant price as the store's LOWEST price.

jsonld.synth_note: LD offer is the DEFAULT variant at 99.00 — deliberately still under a $100 cap, so the wrong answer is a PASS with a false number rather than a flipped verdict.

json_tier.synth_note: prepend a UTF-8 BOM (EF BB BF) to an otherwise valid body.

why: `safeFetch` decodes with `Buffer.concat(chunks).toString("utf8")` (fetch.ts:151), which preserves U+FEFF, and `JSON.parse("﻿{...}")` throws. The throw is swallowed by the tier-2 `catch { }` at productTest.ts:1170. Executed end to end: `fetched.json` is `false`, `attempted` still lists "json", `degraded` stays `false`, and the row renders `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $99.00.` The verdict is accidentally right and the sentence is false — the store's lowest price is $34.00. The word doing the damage is "lowest": the engine read exactly one price and reported it as a minimum over a set it never obtained. `requires_store_access` is the honest verdict because the engine's own doctrine (a measurement that did not complete is not a passing measurement) applies exactly here: an unparsed tier must not be summed as an empty one. Two aggravations worth stating: `degraded` false means this result is CACHED for seven days, and `accessDetail` uses that same flag to decide whether to blame us or the store, so every consequent row blames the merchant.

subclass: content-type rewrite — valid JSON labelled `text/plain`
intent: Have a WAF or CDN relabel the `.json` response so the engine discards a body it downloaded intact, flipping the price verdict.

json_tier.synth_note: body is byte-perfect Shopify product JSON; ONLY the Content-Type header is wrong.

why: The tier-2 guard is `r.status === 200 && /json/i.test(r.contentType ?? "")`; `text/plain` fails it and falls to `else if (r.status === 200) sawNonJson = true`. Executed: `minPriceUsd` 249, row `not_proven | Lowest readable price is $249.00, at or above the $40 requirement.` — a flipped verdict against a store whose cheapest variant is $34.00. The second edge is the diagnosis: `sawNonJson` is what produces the `not_shopify` error ("This looks like it isn't a Shopify store") whenever no other tier answered, so on a store where the page tier is also blocked, one wrong header tells a Shopify merchant they are not on Shopify. Note that `text/plain` is on `safeFetch`'s own ALLOWED_CONTENT_TYPES, so the transport accepts the body and the caller throws it away — the two layers disagree about what a readable response is. Calibration: the corpus does contain 4 `.json` responses with a non-JSON content type, but every one is at status 404 or 429, where the status check rejects them first; the 200 form is what no sample here holds.

subclass: absent Content-Type header on the page tier
intent: Make a live, fully published product page invisible to the engine by omitting one response header, so a real product is reported to its own merchant as not existing.

jsonld.synth_note: the page is complete and valid — JSON-LD Product with name, description, price and availability. The origin server simply sends NO Content-Type header.

must_not_render: We couldn't find a product at that URL.

why: Executed: `errorKind: "not_found"`, message "We couldn't find a product at that URL." The page tier's guard is `/html/i.test(r.contentType ?? "")`, which is false for a null header, so the complete page is discarded without extraction; `.json` 404s, `saw404` is set, `!js && !extracted` holds, and the engine reports the product does not exist. The transport disagrees with the engine about this exact case: `isAllowedContentType(null)` returns `true` on purpose (fetch.ts:58, "missing content-type: allow, but we still byte-cap"), so `safeFetch` downloads the body and the caller silently drops it. This is the sharpest form of the doctrine failure in this cluster, because `not_found` is not a degraded result or an unadjudicated row — it is a positive assertion about the merchant's store, made from a header rather than from content, with a $249 in-stock product sitting in the bytes we hold. Against a $300 cap the true row is a pass.

subclass: content-type mismatch on `.js` — four causes collapse into one boolean
intent: Remove the only tier carrying prices via a wrong Content-Type, and show that the resulting state is byte-identical to a 404, a parse failure and a truncation.

json_tier.synth_note: the `.json` body carries title/body_html/options but NO `variants` key at all, so tier 3 is the only price source and `jsonHasVariantSignal` is false.

js_tier.synth_note: body is valid Shopify `.js` product JSON; only the Content-Type is wrong.

why: The tier-3 guard is `/javascript|json/i.test(r.contentType ?? "")`; `text/html` fails it, so the body is discarded and `usedJsEndpoint` stays false. Executed with a `.json` that carries no variants: `minPriceUsd` falls to the LD 249 and the row renders `not_proven` against a $40 cap for a $34.00 product. The structural point is the reporting state, which I compared across four separate runs: a `.js` 404, a `.js` 200 with a wrong content type, a `.js` 200 whose body fails `JSON.parse`, and a `.js` truncated at the byte cap ALL produce exactly `fetched.js: false`, `attempted` containing "js", `degraded: false`, and no diagnostic field of any kind. Four different facts about the world — the endpoint is gone, we refused it, it was malformed, we cut it off — are indistinguishable downstream, and only one of them is a fact about the store. Contrast tt-13, where a robots skip at least omits "js" from `attempted`. `truncated` is the field that would have separated the fourth: `safeFetch` returns it (fetch.ts:43) and `defaultFetchUrl` (productTest.ts:1005) drops it at the seam.

subclass: byte cap cuts the `.js` body mid-array
intent: Exceed `LIMITS.maxBytes` on the tier that carries both prices and availability, so the whole tier is lost to a parse error caused by our own cut rather than by the store.

js_tier.synth_note: a ~1.72MB `.js` payload (a size/colour matrix of ~900 variants). The harness must apply `LIMITS.maxBytes = 1_500_000` and hand the engine the CUT string, exactly as `safeFetch` does — and must DROP the `truncated` flag, as `defaultFetchUrl` does. The cut lands mid-object inside `variants[]`.

why: Executed with a body cut mid-object: `JSON.parse` throws, the tier-3 `catch { }` swallows it, `usedJsEndpoint` stays false, and with `.json` 404 the price falls to the LD 249 — `not_proven` against a $40 cap for a product whose cheapest variant is $12.00. The mechanism is entirely ours: `safeFetch` computed `truncated: true` and `defaultFetchUrl` returns only `{status, contentType, body, finalUrl}`, so the one bit that distinguishes "the store sent us a broken payload" from "we stopped reading" is destroyed at the seam. `PublicProduct` has no field that can carry it either, so even a fixed fetcher would have nowhere to put it. Honest calibration on reachability, since this is the campaign's headline metric: the largest captured `.js` body across 397 snapshots is 411,896 bytes (reanimatorcoffee.com, 27% of the cap) and the largest variant list is 60 (felixgray.com), so at observed density this needs roughly 220 variants. Possible for a store using Shopify's 2048-variant limit; not something 172 stores would be expected to contain. I mark it unreachable but the numbers are here to be argued with.

subclass: byte cap amputates the page's structured data
intent: Let the test complete normally while the byte cap silently removes the JSON-LD block and the analytics bootstrap, so every structured-data row becomes a false accusation.

jsonld.synth_note: a ~1.66MB product page (heavy theme + inlined reviews). The theme emits BOTH `var meta = {...}` and the JSON-LD Product block in the last 100KB. The harness must apply `LIMITS.maxBytes = 1_500_000` and hand the engine the CUT string. After the cut neither survives.

bootstrap.synth_note: present in the full page, past the cut — so `shopifyMetaObject` returns null and `productType` degrades to null.

must_not_render: This product publishes no Product structured data, so there is no GTIN or MPN for a machine buyer to read.
Your product structured data publishes no GTIN or MPN

why: Executed on a 1.66MB page cut at 1,500,000: `hasProductSchema` false, `extracted.product.offer.price` null, `productType` null, `storefrontObjectId` null, `ldAvailability` null — and no error, `degraded: false`, the test runs to completion. The price row is right by luck (the `.json` tier answers, $34.00 passes) while every row that reads structured data is a false accusation about a store that publishes it correctly. `extractJsonLd`'s regex requires a closing `</script>`, so an amputated block does not merely lose a field, it disappears; `shopifyMetaObject` returns null on an unbalanced brace scan by design. Because `degraded` is false the wrong result is stored by `storeResult` for seven days — the cache deliberately refuses to pin degraded results precisely to avoid "a week-long wrong answer", and no transport failure in this cluster sets that flag. Reachability, measured rather than assumed: 16 of 397 captured pages are AT this cap (corkcicle.com 1,501,617 bytes; bornprimitive, nakednutrition, organicbasics, foursigmatic, knix, brooklinen, misen, origincoffee.co.uk …), and on all 16 the last LD block closed and `var meta` stayed balanced (two-sided canary: 16 at the cap, 364 far under). So the precondition occurs in real samples 16 times and only the theme's script ordering separates those stores from this case. brooklinen.com and misen.com show zero LD blocks in their truncated bodies, and from the snapshot alone it is not decidable whether they publish none or lost them to the cut — which is the indistinguishability this case is about.

subclass: the extractor's own 512KB per-block cap, on an untruncated page
intent: Deliver a complete, valid page whose single JSON-LD block exceeds `MAX_JSONLD_BYTES`, so the parser skips it with `continue` and the page reads as publishing nothing.

jsonld.synth_note: ONE `<script type="application/ld+json">` block of ~600KB — a Product node with several hundred inlined `Review` nodes, which is what a reviews app produces. The page arrives COMPLETE and well under the 1.5MB transport cap; a `<meta name="description">` is present so the evidence index is non-empty and no error fires.

must_not_render: This product publishes no Product structured data
No public price is exposed on this product.

why: `extractJsonLd` (extract.ts:87) does `if (!blob || blob.length > MAX_JSONLD_BYTES) continue;` with `MAX_JSONLD_BYTES = 512_000`. Executed: `title` null, `hasProductSchema` false, `minPriceUsd` null, no error raised, and no price row survives into a generated task at all (`adjudicability` returns 0 for a null price, so the candidate is dropped at :1615 — the row does not become `requires_store_access`, it ceases to exist). Under a pinned cap it returns `requires_store_access | No public price is exposed on this product.` about a store that publishes price, availability and a GTIN in valid schema.org markup. This is a distinct mechanism from tt-08: nothing was truncated, no header was wrong, no tier failed — a hard-coded parser limit chose not to read a document that arrived whole, and it does so silently because `continue` is indistinguishable from a block that was not a Product. The cap is a defensible safety choice; reporting the consequence as the merchant's failure to publish is not. Measured: 0 of 397 captured pages carry a JSON-LD block over 512KB, so no sample here reaches it.

subclass: redirect chain lands on a DIFFERENT product; `finalUrl` is discarded
intent: Have the requested handle 301 to another product, so a single request produces a complete verdict about the wrong product published under the requested URL.

jsonld.synth_note: the request is for /products/blue-mug (a retired $18 handle). It 301s to /products/red-mug, whose page is complete: LD Product with name, description, price 42 and InStock. The JSON-LD, title and all prose belong to RED mug. `finalUrl` is set on the page response.

json_tier.synth_note: /products/blue-mug.json — the retired handle has no API record.

why: `finalUrl` is consulted in exactly one place — the robots.txt fetch, to move `canonicalOrigin` (productTest.ts:1093). The page tier ignores it entirely. Executed: the result is titled with the OTHER product's name, `minPriceUsd` is the other product's 42, and `product.origin`/`productUrl` remain the requested URL, so a citable result asserts facts about blue-mug that were read from red-mug. Worse, `pageSufficient` is true here (node + prose + price + availability), so tiers 2 and 3 are never requested — `attempted` is `["page"]` and ONE request decided the entire verdict. The honest answer is `requires_store_access` with a null price: the requested product was never read, and the engine has the evidence to know that (it holds a `finalUrl` whose path differs from the one it asked for). Reachability is measured, and it is the uncomfortable answer: 17 of 397 captured page responses redirect to a different path, and 4 land on a plainly different product — misen.com `/products/chefs-knife-alternate` → `/products/chefs-knife`, wildone.com `/products/dog-harness` → `/products/cushioned-dog-harness`, tecovas.com `/products/the-claire-braid-midnight-suede` → `/products/the-claire-braid`, bollandbranch.com's sheet-set variant handle → the base set. Replayed through the engine, wildone.com yields `pass_evidenced | Price under $50 | Lowest readable price is $48.00.` under the requested handle. The sample CONTAINED this and every rendered row looks ordinary, which is why no audit here ever saw it.

subclass: redirect lands on the store HOMEPAGE while the API tiers still answer
intent: Split the result across two documents — prose and claims judged against the homepage, price and variants read from the requested product's API — so every claim row becomes a false accusation inside an otherwise correct test.

jsonld.ld_note: the landed document is the STORE HOMEPAGE: a <title> of "Reusable Silicone Food Storage & Sandwich Bags | Merchant", a marketing meta description, no Product node.
jsonld.synth_note: request /products/bowl-2-pack; the storefront 302s to / with status 200 on the final hop.

json_tier.synth_note: the requested handle STILL resolves through the API — this is the split that makes the case. body_html states "BPA-free, dishwasher safe silicone".

must_not_render: Checked page description — no statement an AI buyer could verify.
Reusable Silicone Food Storage & Sandwich Bags | Merchant

why: Measured on real captured stores, not hypothesised. Five snapshots redirect a product URL to `/` at status 200: nativeunion.com, popovleather.com, stasherbag.com, equator.ca, grind.co.uk. Replayed through the engine today, stasherbag.com returns a complete 8-row test whose `productName` is the homepage `<title>` and whose first row is `not_proven | BPA-free | Checked page description — no statement an AI buyer could verify.` — an accusation about a product page the engine never opened. equator.ca is the exact split this case encodes: the page tier landed on `/` while `/products/peru-geisha-microlot-w.json` still answered, so the result carries `pass_evidenced | Price under $20 | Lowest readable price is $16.00.` and `pass_evidenced | 175g option available` from the correct product alongside `not_proven | Single-origin` judged against the homepage. That mixture is the hazard: the correct rows lend credibility to the false ones, and the merchant has no way to tell which document each row came from. The price verdict here is genuinely a pass, so `honest_answer.verdict` is `pass` — the defect lives in the claim rows and in `productName`, and the honest engine must refuse to adjudicate any prose row after a redirect whose path is not the requested one.

subclass: robots.txt cross-host redirect moves `canonicalOrigin`
intent: Use the robots.txt fetch — the one place `finalUrl` IS honoured — to move every subsequent request onto a host that is not the merchant's storefront.

jsonld.synth_note: THE REQUEST IS FOR https://merchant.example/products/kettle. merchant.example/robots.txt 301s to partner-cdn.example/robots.txt. The jsonld/json_tier described here are what partner-cdn.example serves at /products/kettle — a DIFFERENT retailer's listing of a similar kettle at $119. merchant.example's own page (its kettle is $64, one variant) is never requested.

json_tier.synth_note: partner-cdn.example/products/kettle.json — not needed, the page is sufficient there.

why: productTest.ts:1090-1095 reassigns `canonicalOrigin` from the robots.txt `finalUrl` whenever the host differs, and every later tier is built as `${canonicalOrigin}${path}`. Executed: only two requests are issued — the merchant's robots.txt and the OTHER host's product page — and `product.origin` is returned as the other host, so the result is stamped with a store the merchant does not own. The feature is deliberate and useful (apex→www), but the redirect target is attacker- or accident-controlled and there is no check that the destination is the same registrable domain, the same storefront, or even a Shopify store. The honest verdict is `requires_store_access`: nothing from merchant.example was ever read, so no claim about its kettle is supportable. Reachability, measured: 127 of 396 captured robots.txt responses redirect cross-host, and 8 of those cross a different registrable domain — cocofloss.com→cocolab.com, ridgewallet.com→ridge.com, wandpdesign.com→wandp.com, yellowbirdsauce.com→yellowbirdfoods.com, agroroasters.com→agrocoffee.com, caravancoffeeroasters.co.uk→caravanandco.com, irvingfarm.com→irvingfarmcoffee.com, peetscoffee.com→peets.com. All eight are rebrands where the destination IS the same merchant, so the mechanism is demonstrably live on real stores while the harmful destination is not in the sample.

subclass: robots disallows `/products/*.js$` — forbidden to look, reported as looked
intent: Block only tier 3 through robots, so absent `available` flags default to true and the engine names a sold-out variant as the lowest price a buyer can pay — in a sentence byte-identical to the one it renders when it WAS allowed to look.

jsonld.synth_note: the anchored `$` form blocks ONLY the .js endpoint — verified: page allowed, .json allowed, .js disallowed. `availability` absent from the LD so tier 3 would otherwise fire.

js_tier.synth_note: THE ENGINE MUST NEVER REQUEST THIS — robots forbids it. It is specified so the honest answer is checkable: Small is SOLD OUT.

must_not_render: At least one variant is listed as purchasable.

why: This is the `requires_store_access` doctrine tested in the direction the engine gets wrong. Executed both ways on the same store: with robots blocking `.js`, variant availability comes back `[true, true]`; with robots allowing it, `[false, true]`. The default is `available: v.available !== false`, so an ABSENT flag becomes a stated `true` — and `available` is absent from 1141 of 1141 captured `.json` variants, making tier 3 the only availability source on essentially every store. Both runs render the identical sentence `Lowest readable price is $34.00.` The merchant cannot distinguish them, and $34.00 is a price no buyer can pay; the cheapest purchasable variant is $58.00, which is ABOVE a $40 cap, so the verdict flips too. Nothing records the refusal: `attempted` simply omits "js", `degraded` stays false, and `robotsStatus` reports "ok" because robots.txt itself was fetched fine. `degraded` false is load-bearing twice over — `accessDetail` uses it to decide whether to blame us or the store, so the engine actively attributes its own blindness to the merchant, and the result is cached for seven days. The engine's own error copy proves it knows the distinction: `robots_disallowed` says "This store asks automated tools not to read this page, and we respect that" — but that error only fires when BOTH the page and `.json` are blocked (:1110), never for a single tier. Measured: 0 of 396 captured robots.txt files carry any `/products/*.js` rule.

subclass: unanchored `Disallow: /products/*.js` silently blocks `.json` too
intent: Write the robots rule a merchant would naturally write to block the JS endpoint, and take out BOTH product-data tiers because the pattern is compiled without an end anchor.

jsonld.synth_note: NO `$`. The LD offer is the DEFAULT (largest) variant at 249 — the store's real cheapest variant is 34.00 and lives only in the .json tier.

json_tier.synth_note: THE ENGINE MUST NEVER REQUEST THIS — robots (accidentally) forbids it. Specified so the honest answer is checkable.

why: Executed against `parseRobots`/`isAllowedByRobots` directly: `Disallow: /products/*.js` yields page=allowed, **.json=DISALLOWED**, .js=disallowed, while `Disallow: /products/*.js$` yields .json=allowed. The cause is `matchesPath` (robots.ts:77-85): it compiles the pattern to `^/products/.*\.js` and only appends `$` when the pattern ends with one, so `/products/widget.json` matches the unanchored form because `.json` begins with `.js`. Executed end to end, the store is read from the page alone — `attempted` is `["page"]`, `minPriceUsd` is the LD 249, and the row renders `not_proven | Lowest readable price is $249.00, at or above the $40 requirement.` about a store whose cheapest variant is $34.00. Two tiers die from one line, and the `robots_disallowed` error cannot fire because it requires the page path to be blocked as well, so the engine proceeds as though nothing was refused. This is a pure pattern-semantics defect: no amount of real-store sampling can find it, because the rule is correct robots syntax that our matcher reads more broadly than the author meant. Measured: 0 of 396 captured robots.txt files carry the rule in either form.

subclass: password-protected storefront answers 200 on every tier
intent: Serve the Shopify password page at every tier with status 200, so the engine names the store from an interstitial and adjudicates a product test against it.

jsonld.ld_note: the landed document is the password gate: <title>Merchant — Opening soon</title>, <meta name="description" content="Enter store using password">, a password form. No Product node.

json_tier.synth_note: /products/{handle}.json also returns the password page HTML at status 200 — this is what a locked storefront does.

must_not_render: no statement an AI buyer could verify
This product exposes no availability data publicly.

why: Executed: no error is raised — `extracted` is truthy because the password page has a title and a meta description, so `readSomething` is satisfied by the evidence index. The result is returned with `storeName`/`productName` taken from the interstitial ("Merchant — Opening soon"), `degraded: false`, and every claim row rendering `not_proven | ... no statement an AI buyer could verify` about copy behind a gate. `requires_store_access` is the entire meaning of this status and it is exactly what should fire; instead the engine produces its harshest real output. The signals to detect it are in the bytes we already hold: a `finalUrl` of `/password` and a `.json` tier returning HTML. Note the interaction with tt-04: because the `.json` HTML is served as `text/html`, `sawNonJson` is set, so on a locked store where the page tier also fails the merchant is told "This looks like it isn't a Shopify store" — the one thing we can be certain is false, since only Shopify serves this gate. Reachability: a capture campaign records stores that answered with product pages, so a password-walled storefront is excluded by construction — the sample cannot contain the shape no matter how large it grows.

subclass: duplicate JSON keys — `JSON.parse` keeps the last
intent: Put two `price` keys in one variant object so the engine silently adopts the second and publishes a price an order of magnitude below the real one.

json_tier.synth_note: the Small variant object must literally contain `"price":"34.00", ... ,"price":"3.40"` — two `price` keys in one object. This is what a middlebox that string-splices a promo price into the body produces; it is valid to every JSON parser and lossy in all of them.

why: Executed: `minPriceUsd` is 3.4 and the row renders `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $3.40.` The RFC-8259 rule is that duplicate names are permitted and behaviour is implementation-defined; V8 keeps the last. The verdict is accidentally right (both figures are under a $40 cap) and the published number is wrong by 10×, in the direction that makes a merchant's product look mispriced to an AI buyer citing our result. The wider point is that this is unrepairable downstream: by the time `js.variants` exists the first value is gone, so no validation, linter or audit that reads the parsed object can ever detect it — only a check against the raw bytes could, and the raw bytes are discarded at the seam. Note this is also the one case in this cluster a rendered-evidence audit CAN see, since the sentence carries a number a human would question — which is precisely why the quoteless rows this repo already documents are the more dangerous shape.

subclass: `.js` redirect returns another handle's payload, merged into this product
intent: Have the `.js` request land on a different product so its variants REPLACE the correct ones while the title, vendor and options stay behind — one object holding two products.

json_tier.synth_note: correct payload for the requested handle: title "Probe Widget", body_html, and the two real variants. No `available` flags, so tier 3 fires.

js_tier.synth_note: a Shopify URL Redirect on the handle sends /products/widget.js to /products/gift-card.js, which returns the GIFT CARD's payload: handle "gift-card", title "Gift Card", one variant at 500 cents ($5.00).

why: The merge is `js = js ? { ...js, variants: dotJs.variants } : dotJs` (productTest.ts:1211). It replaces the variant array wholesale with no check that the payload describes the same product — `dotJs.handle` and `dotJs.id` are both present in the body and neither is compared to the requested handle. Executed: the result keeps `title: "Probe Widget"` from the `.json` tier and takes `minPriceUsd: 500` from the gift card, rendering `not_proven | Lowest readable price is $500.00, at or above the $40 requirement.` for a $34.00 product. Two defects stack: the object now describes two products at once (title and options from one, prices and availability from the other, with no field recording the split), and the gift card's `500` cents sits below the cents guard's `p > 1000` threshold, so $5.00 publishes as $500.00. `fetched.js` reports `true`, so every diagnostic says the tier answered — which it did, about something else. Distinct from tt-10: there the wrong document replaces the right one, here it is spliced into it, and the surviving correct fields are what make the result look coherent.

subclass: deeply nested JSON-LD blows the stack and discards the ENTIRE page tier
intent: Include one pathologically nested ld+json block so `flattenLd` throws a RangeError outside the per-block guard, taking the whole page — including a valid Product node in a second block — with it.

jsonld.synth_note: BLOCK 1 is a ~40,000-deep nested JSON array (`[[[[...1...]]]]`) — valid JSON, under the 512KB cap, emitted by a misbehaving third-party app. BLOCK 2 is a correct Product node with name, description, price 34.00, InStock and a GTIN. Block order matters: the nested block comes first.

bootstrap.synth_note: `var meta` is present and well-formed on the page — and is lost anyway, because the whole page tier is discarded.

must_not_render: This product publishes no Product structured data
no statement of what this product is made of that an AI buyer could read

why: Executed twice. Directly: `extractPage(html)` throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`. `extractJsonLd`'s try/catch is per-block and wraps only `JSON.parse` — the parse of a deep array SUCCEEDS; the overflow happens afterwards in `flattenLd`'s recursive `visit`, which is outside every guard. Through the engine: the page tier's blanket `catch { /* the JSON tier is the fallback */ }` at :1147 swallows it, `fetched.page` is `false`, and the VALID Product block in the same document, the meta description, the FAQ, `product_type` and `storefrontObjectId` are all lost — the page's failure is total, not partial, and silent. The price row survives only because the `.json` tier happens to answer; had it 404'd the store would have been reported `unreachable`. Two properties make this worth a case rather than a curiosity: the blast radius is the whole document rather than the offending block, which is the opposite of how the per-block guard was clearly intended to behave; and the input is merchant-adjacent rather than merchant-authored — a review, recipe or bundle app emitting recursive `@graph` structures reaches it without anyone at the store doing anything. Measured: 0 instances across 397 captured pages.

subclass: tier 3 REPLACES tier 2 wholesale — the correct string was already in hand and was discarded
intent: Make the engine throw away a price it had already read correctly, by publishing the same true price in both tiers in the two encodings each tier really uses.
why: Both tiers describe one $10.00 mug. Tier 2 says "10.00" (string dollars) and tier 3 says 1000 (integer cents) — the two encodings the corpus shows are universal and type-disjoint (1141/1141 .json prices string, 1042/1042 .js prices number). The engine fetches tier 2, converts it correctly to 10, then reaches `js = js ? { ...js, variants: dotJs.variants } : dotJs` and REPLACES the whole variant list with tier 3's. `priceToUsd`'s cents guard is `p > 1000 && Number.isInteger(p)`, a strict `>` on the exact boundary, so 1000 stays 1000 and the merchant is told $1000.00. Executed: `minPriceUsd: 1000`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $1000.00.` The honest answer is $10.00 because the store publishes exactly one price and both surfaces agree on it. This case is the cluster's anchor rather than a novelty: v3.7 already found the 100x class on levainbakery.com. What it adds is the framing — the engine did not fail to read the price, it read it and then overwrote it with a tier it trusts more for a reason (availability) that has nothing to do with price.

subclass: an EMPTY tier-3 variant list silently erases a complete tier-2 price list
intent: Make a junk-but-well-typed .js payload delete a correct price list and push the answer onto a third surface nobody was reading.
why: `Array.isArray([])` is true, so the guard that is supposed to reject a malformed .js payload admits an empty one: `js = { ...js, variants: [] }`. `prices` is then empty and `minPriceUsd` falls through to `ld?.offer?.price` — the JSON-LD number, which on a real store is routinely a compare-at/MSRP/parent price rather than the sell price. Executed: `nVariants: 0`, `minPriceUsd: 99`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $99.00.`, and `fetched.js` reports `true`. The honest answer is $34.00 because that is what tier 2 published and no public surface contradicts it; the $99 is the LD figure the store never asks a buyer to pay. Note the shape of the failure: a 404 and a 429 on the same tier both KEEP the tier-2 answer (executed as controls: both render $34.00). Only a 200 with a well-typed empty list destroys it — the success path is the dangerous one.

subclass: tier-3 variants with no price erase tier 2's prices AND leave phantom purchasable variants behind
intent: Split the two things a variant carries — its price and its existence — across tiers, so the engine keeps the existence claim from the tier that has no prices and the price from a tier that describes nothing.
why: Same replacement line as tier-02, but the list is non-empty, so the damage is two-sided. `priceToUsd(null)` returns null (typeof null is "object", not "number" or "string"), so `prices` is empty and `minPriceUsd` falls back to the LD 129 — while `variants` now holds TWO entries whose `available` is computed as `v.available !== false`, i.e. an ABSENT flag becomes a stated `true`. Executed: `variantPrices: [null, null]`, `minPriceUsd: 129`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $129.00.`, plus `In stock and purchasable | At least one variant is listed as purchasable.` derived from variants that carry no price and no availability at all. The honest answer is $8.50: that is the only price any public surface states for this product. The general lesson is that the tier merge is not a merge — the two halves of a variant record (identity, price) travel together and are replaced together, so a tier that is authoritative for one is treated as authoritative for both.

subclass: tier 3 lists a SUBSET of tier 2's variants and the missing one is the cheapest
intent: Make the engine publish a minimum computed over a list it can see is shorter than the one it already fetched.
why: Executed: `minPriceUsd: 24`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $24.00.` The engine holds three publicly published prices and reports the minimum of one of them, because the replacement is unconditional — there is no length check, no union, and no reconciliation. A shorter list is exactly what a market-scoped or availability-filtered .js payload would return, and it is indistinguishable from a complete one. The honest answer is $9.00: the Small variant is listed at a public, robots-allowed endpoint the engine successfully read in the same run. Worth noting what makes this invisible downstream: the rendered sentence is a plausible price for a plausible product, and there is no quote to audit — the v3.2 'a row that renders no quote is invisible to a human audit' failure mode applies to every price row, not just identifiers.

subclass: CONTROL — one boolean about availability suppresses tier 3, and the price becomes correct
intent: Prove the tier-3 gate is load-bearing on PRICE by flipping a field that says nothing about price, and pin the correct answer so a fix cannot be scored against a shifting baseline.
why: This case must PASS today and must keep passing. `jsonHasVariantSignal = (js?.variants ?? []).some(v => typeof v.available === "boolean")` — one boolean anywhere in the tier-2 variant array suppresses the tier-3 fetch entirely. Executed: tiers asked are robots + page + .json only, `minPriceUsd: 8.5`, row `Lowest readable price is $8.50.` — correct. Delete the single `available: true` and the identical store publishes $850.00 (executed: `minPriceUsd: 850`). So a field that describes stock decides whether the price is right by two orders of magnitude, and the merchant has no way to know which branch they are on. This is an anchor in the sense the repo's mutation proof means: without it, a fix to the cents guard alone would look like it closed the class while the tier-selection defect underneath it stayed live and undetected. It is also the reason the gate is not a rare path — measured, 0 of 1141 captured .json variants carry an `available` key at all, so tier 3 fires on essentially every store that lacks JSON-LD availability. The brief's "available is OFTEN ABSENT" understates it: it is always absent, which inverts tier 3 from a fallback into the default.

subclass: the tier-3 gate is keyed on AVAILABILITY, so an availability-only tier permanently blocks the only tier with prices
intent: Give tier 2 the one field the gate reads and none of the fields the row needs, so the engine locks itself out of the prices and answers from a third surface entirely.
why: Executed: tiers asked are robots + page + .json; `variantPrices: [null, null]`; `minPriceUsd: 129`; row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $129.00.` The gate asks a question about availability and uses the answer to decide a question about price. Here tier 2 answers the availability question definitively and carries no prices at all, so tier 3 — which has both — is never requested, and the engine falls back past both variant tiers onto the LD figure. The honest answer is $19.00, published at `/products/{handle}.js`, a robots-allowed public endpoint the engine fetches on 145 of the captured stores and declined to fetch here for a reason unrelated to price. This is the sharpest form of the precondition attack because nothing is malformed: every field present is true, and the row is wrong by $110 anyway.

subclass: JSON-LD availability suppresses tier 3, tier 2 is gone, and the price row DISAPPEARS from the report
intent: Make the engine decline to fetch the one tier that carries the price, then tell the merchant no public price exists — about a store that publishes one.

must_not_render: No public price is exposed on this product.

why: `if (!ldAvailability && !jsonHasVariantSignal)` gates the tier-3 fetch. The page publishes availability but no price, so `pageSufficient` is false (it needs a price) and tier 2 is attempted — and 404s. `ldAvailability` is nevertheless set, so tier 3 is never asked. Executed: tiers asked are robots + page + .json; `minPriceUsd: null`. With a generated task the row is not deferred, it is DROPPED — `adjudicability` returns 0 for a null price and the candidate is filtered out, so the merchant's report simply has no price row and nothing says why (executed: 6 rows, no price row). Pin the requirement and it renders `requires_store_access | No public price is exposed on this product.` — a false statement about a store whose price is one robots-allowed GET away. The honest answer is $24.00, pass. The direction of the error matters: every other case here makes the engine say something wrong; this one makes it say nothing, and nothing is what a store with no public data also produces.

subclass: `pageSufficient` publishes the page's own number and never fetches the tier that would refute it
intent: Satisfy the sufficiency predicate exactly, so the engine stops after one request and reports a single-variant LD price as the MINIMUM of a multi-variant product.

jsonld.description: A pre-seasoned cast iron skillet, made in the USA.

why: `pageSufficient = pageHasNode && pageHasText && offer.price != null && Boolean(offer.availability)`. All four hold, so tiers 2 and 3 are never requested. Executed: tiers asked are robots + page ONLY; `minPriceUsd: 135`; row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $135.00.` — which is the product's MAXIMUM. The honest answer is $79.00, published on two public endpoints the engine chose not to spend a request on. Remove `availability` from the same store and the engine fetches both tiers and answers $79.00 (executed). One optional LD field decides whether the reported minimum is the minimum. The reason this belongs in a chosen-input campaign despite being common: 234 of the 397 captured products fetched NO variant tier at all, so for 59% of the corpus the bytes that would refute the published number were never captured. Only 3 of 397 snapshots contain both a sufficient page and a variant tier, and 2 of those 3 disagree (september.coffee: LD 24 vs variant minimum 28.50). A real-store audit is not merely unlikely to catch this class — it is structurally incapable of it, because the refutation is exactly the request the predicate exists to avoid.

subclass: market-localized JSON-LD vs default-market variant tier — one optional field flips both the number and the currency
intent: Publish two true prices for one product in two currencies on two tiers, and make a single LD field decide which one the merchant is shown, with neither labelled.

jsonld.description: An Ethiopian natural, roasted for filter.
jsonld.note: the LD offer is emitted for the /en-us/ market context

bootstrap.note: published as top-level `Shopify.currency = {"active":"CAD"}` and `Shopify.country = "CA"`, which no code path reads

why: Executed both branches. With `availability` present the page is sufficient, nothing else is fetched, and the row reads `Lowest readable price is $24.00.` — a US-market number for a merchant on a CAD storefront. Remove `availability` (or empty the LD `description`, which is what the real store does) and the engine reads tier 2 and renders `Lowest readable price is $28.50.` — the right market's number wearing a US dollar sign. Neither sentence is true as written: the first is another market's price, the second is CA$28.50 rendered as $28.50, and nothing in `productTest.ts` reads a currency at all (`offer.currency` IS parsed in `extract.ts:126` and reaches `PublicProduct`; a repo-wide grep finds zero readers of it in the test engine). The honest answer for the URL the merchant pasted is CA$28.50 — the price its own default market charges — and it must be rendered with its currency named or not rendered as a price at all. This is drawn from september.coffee, captured in both coffee sets with exactly LD `price: 24, priceCurrency: "USD"` against `.json` `"28.50"`; it is the only LD-vs-variant-tier price disagreement in 397 snapshots and no audit has ever looked at it.

subclass: one JSON-LD Product node PER VARIANT, and the node emitted first is not the cheapest
intent: Make the page tier's node SELECTION, not its content, produce a maximum reported as a minimum — with the cheaper node visible in the same HTML.
why: `extractProduct` is `nodes.find(n => isType(n, "Product") || isType(n, "ProductGroup"))` — the FIRST Product node in document order across every ld+json block, with no tie-break on completeness, name match, or price. The King node is complete, so `pageSufficient` fires and tiers 2 and 3 are never requested. Executed: tiers asked are robots + page only; `minPriceUsd: 299`; row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $299.00.` — for a product whose $229.00 offer is in the very next script tag on the same page. The honest answer is $229.00 from the page's own markup. Measured basis for calling this unreachable by sampling rather than merely rare: 56 of 397 captured pages carry more than one Product node, exactly one (bollandbranch.com, which emits precisely this per-variant pattern) has differing prices among them, and there the first node carries NO price — so the engine falls through and the defect never fires. The corpus contains the markup pattern and, by accident of node order, never the consequence.

subclass: a recommendation widget's Product node is selected as THE product, and sufficiency stops the run there
intent: Put a different product's complete JSON-LD ahead of the page's own, so the engine answers about a product the merchant did not ask about and never checks a tier that would contradict it.

extra_product_nodes_before.name: Copper Kettle Pro
extra_product_nodes_before.description: A 1.7 litre copper kettle with a rapid-boil element.
extra_product_nodes_before.note: emitted by a 'you may also like' widget, before the page's own node

why: Executed: tiers asked are robots + page only; `ldOfferPrice: 899`; `ldCur: "USD"`; row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $899.00.` The selection rule has no aboutness test whatsoever — it is document order — and once the wrong node is selected it is also COMPLETE, so `pageSufficient` fires and the two tiers that describe the right product are never requested. Every downstream row inherits the substitution: identifiers, availability and the task summary all come from the other product. The honest answer is $24.00. This is the price-path instance of the node-selection family v3.5 already filed as P-15 for identifiers, which is why it is worth pinning here: the same `nodes.find(...)` is the sole authority for price, availability, GTIN and MPN, and a fix for one is a fix for all four. Measured: 8 of 397 captured pages carry Product nodes with differing names, and every one is the SAME product duplicated (HTML-entity variants of one title, or per-variant nodes). No captured page emits a different product's node first, so the sample can neither confirm nor deny the class.

subclass: a robots rule aimed at asset files decides which price ENCODING the engine reads
intent: Use the merchant's own robots.txt — a file about crawler courtesy — to route the engine onto the tier whose encoding it mishandles.

jsonld.description: A beeswax food wrap, three pack.

why: The robots gate only ERRORS when both the page and the .json path are disallowed; disallowing one silently skips that tier. Executed with `Disallow: /*.json$`: tiers asked are robots + page + .js; `minPriceUsd: 950`; row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $950.00.` — and `optionValues` comes back empty too, because options live only on the tier that was skipped. Executed with the mirror rule `Disallow: /*.js$`: tiers asked are robots + page + .json; row `Lowest readable price is $9.50.` — correct. The honest answer is $9.50 in both configurations; robots.txt governs what a crawler may request, not what the merchant charges, and a rule written to keep bots off asset files must not change the reported price by 100x. The mirror half of this is REAL — kytebaby.com in the general sample ships `Disallow: /*.js$`, which blocks the product endpoint as collateral and, by luck, is the half that produces the right answer. Measured: 0 of 397 captured robots.txt files block `/products/{handle}.json`, so only chosen input can pose the damaging direction of a rule one character different from one a real merchant already ships.

subclass: a malformed field on one tier CRASHES a test the other two tiers could have answered
intent: Show the tiers are not independent — make tier 2 return a well-formed JSON body with a wrongly-typed field and take down tiers 1 and 3 with it.

json_tier.note: `variants` is a JSON OBJECT keyed by index, not an array — emit it verbatim, do not coerce

must_not_render: (any unhandled exception: every other tier failure in this fetcher degrades to a typed error — 404 → not_found, 429/403 → rate_limited, non-JSON → not_shopify — and this one alone escapes as a crash)

why: Executed: `TypeError: ((intermediate value) ?? []).some is not a function`, thrown out of `fetchPublicProduct`, straight through `runProductTest`, to the route at `src/server/index.ts:664` which records `errorKind: "exception"` and rethrows — an HTTP 500. The throw site is `const jsonHasVariantSignal = (js?.variants ?? []).some(...)`, which sits BEFORE the tier-3 fetch, so the tier holding a perfectly good price is never requested; `(js?.variants ?? []).map(...)` twenty lines later would throw the same way. `?? []` guards null and undefined and nothing else, and `JSON.parse` will hand back any type the body declares. The honest answer is $9.00 — three public surfaces state it and one of them is well-formed. This is the only non-typed failure I found anywhere in the fetch path: every other tier outcome degrades honestly, which is the design, and one wrongly-typed field defeats all of it. Measured: 0 of 162 captured .json product objects carry a non-array `variants`, so nothing but chosen input reaches it — a headless middleware, an app proxy, or any non-Shopify storefront answering the same path does.

subclass: a REFUSED tier picks the encoding, and the sentence built on it carries no hedge
intent: Have the store throttle the tier that would have been read correctly, so the answer comes from the fallback and the merchant sees a confident sentence with no sign that anything was refused.

jsonld.description: A silicone stretch lid, six pack.

why: Executed: `throttled: ["json"]`, `degraded: true` on the result envelope — and the row reads `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $950.00.` with no qualification at all. §2.3's honesty rule is implemented as `accessDetail`, which is reachable ONLY from the `requires_store_access` branch; a `pass_evidenced` price sentence composed from a degraded fetch is never touched by it. So the rule that exists to stop the engine speaking with certainty about surfaces it could not read does not cover the case where it read a DIFFERENT surface instead and got a different answer. The honest answer is $9.50. A 429 on this tier is not exotic — andieswim.com in the general sample is exactly `.json` 429 + `.js` 200, and the v1.1 smoke run is why the tier order was reversed in the first place. What is unreachable is a merchant or an auditor NOTICING, because the only trace is a boolean on the envelope that no rendered row mentions; the number itself looks like a price a store might charge.

subclass: options come from tier 2 and variants from tier 3, so one row contradicts the object it was computed from
intent: Split the two halves of a variant row across tiers so the engine denies the existence of an option it is simultaneously publishing.

must_not_render: Checked the public variant list — no "1kg" variant found.

why: `js = js ? { ...js, variants: dotJs.variants } : dotJs` replaces `variants` and KEEPS `options`, so `optionValues` is computed from tier 2 while `variants` comes from tier 3. Executed with a pinned `variant_option` requirement for "1kg": `optionValues: ["250g","1kg"]` and the row renders `not_proven | Checked the public variant list — no "1kg" variant found.` The engine denies, in one sentence, the existence of a value it is holding in the same `PublicProduct` — and the phrase "the public variant list" is doing the damage, because there were two of them and it read the shorter. The honest answer is that a 1kg variant IS publicly listed, at $18.00 minimum for the product. This is the same replacement line as tier-04 with the price consequence swapped for a self-contradiction consequence, which is worth pinning separately: a fix that only reconciles PRICES across tiers leaves this row exactly as wrong, and this row is the one a merchant can check by hand in five seconds and lose all trust over.

subclass: the two variant tiers publish DIFFERENT prices for the same product, and the tiebreak is undocumented precedence
intent: Force the engine to choose between two contradictory public surfaces and see whether it discloses that it chose.

json_tier.note: the freshly-priced surface — the merchant dropped the price this morning; both tiers are HTTP 200, both robots-allowed, fetched seconds apart, and nothing public says which is current

js_tier.note: a stale CDN copy of the pre-drop price

why: Executed: `minPriceUsd: 24`, row `pass_evidenced | Lowest readable price is $24.00.` The engine silently prefers tier 3 and states the result as fact. The honest answer is that public data does not decide it: two endpoints of the same storefront, both HTTP 200, both robots-allowed, fetched seconds apart, state different prices for one product, and there is no public signal — no timestamp, no cache header the engine keeps, no cross-check — that ranks one over the other. `requires_store_access` is exactly what this engine's own honesty discipline calls that state, and it is what an engine that noticed would return; the current answer is not a measurement but an implementation detail of a line whose purpose was to fill in an availability flag. Note the reverse configuration also renders confidently and happens to be RIGHT (executed: stale tier 2 at "24.00" + fresh tier 3 at 1899 → $18.99), which is worse than being wrong twice, because it means the class cannot be detected by comparing the engine's answer to reality on any single store. Measured: across the 144 snapshots that captured both variant tiers, 0 disagree by even a cent — real stores serve both endpoints off the same Liquid render, so only chosen input can ask this question at all.

subclass: a 404 (not a 429) on the copy-bearing tier turns "we could not read it" into "you publish nothing"
intent: Lose the tier that carries the product copy through a status the engine does not count as degradation, and make it accuse the merchant of publishing nothing.

json_tier.body_html: The serving bowl is made from 18/10 stainless steel and is dishwasher safe. It measures 10 inches across and weighs 2.4 lb. Ships in 2-3 business days.
json_tier.note: this copy is what the tier WOULD have served; the case is that a 404 hides it

must_not_render: Checked product title and page description — no statement of what this product is made of that an AI buyer could read.
Checked product title and page description — no readable measurements — size, capacity, weight or fit.
No delivery timing in your public product data

why: Executed as a matched pair on one store. With tier 2 at 200: `Materials are stated | Stated in your product copy.`, `Measurements are stated | Stated in your product copy.`, `Delivery timing is stated in your product copy.` — three passes. With tier 2 at 404 and everything else identical: `descriptionText` is empty (tier 3's payload has no `body_html`), `degraded` is **false** because only 429/403 set it, `fetched.json` reports **true** because it means "we have a product object", not "the .json tier answered" — and the same three rows become flat accusations that the merchant publishes no materials, no measurements and no delivery timing. Contrast the 429 branch, executed on the same store, which correctly renders the throttle disclosure. So the honesty rule keys on the store REFUSING us rather than on the copy-bearing tier not answering, and a 404 slips between them. The honest answer is that all three attributes are publicly stated — 140 of the 162 captured .json bodies carry a substantial `body_html`, so this is where most stores' product copy actually lives — and the price is $45.00. Measured on reachability: 8 captured stores 404'd their .json, and in exactly one (summersalt.com) did .js answer, where the body was the literal `null` so no product was assembled; no captured store reaches the state where the engine assembles a product with empty copy off a 404 and then makes the accusation.

subclass: the page tier's redirect does not move the origin, so tier 1 describes a different page than tiers 2 and 3
intent: Let the product URL redirect somewhere else while the variant tiers keep answering from the original host, so the engine merges two products into one report.

jsonld.description: A 1.7 litre copper kettle with a rapid-boil element.
jsonld.note: this markup belongs to the REDIRECT TARGET; the requested product URL 302s to it and `finalUrl` is consulted only for robots.txt

json_tier.note: served from the ORIGINAL host — the product the merchant actually asked about

why: `canonicalOrigin` is moved ONLY by robots.txt's `finalUrl` (`productTest.ts:1081-1107`); the page tier's own `finalUrl` is never read, so a product URL that redirects elsewhere yields the target's HTML parsed as this product's page while tiers 2 and 3 keep answering from the requested host. Executed: the target's LD is a complete Product, `pageSufficient` fires, tiers 2 and 3 are never requested, and the whole report is about the other product — `minPriceUsd: 189`, row `Lowest readable price is $189.00.`, and even the task line reads "Find the Copper Kettle Pro…" for a URL that resolves to an $18.00 mug. Executed with `availability` removed from the target's LD: tiers 2 and 3 ARE fetched and the result is a chimera — `title: "Enamel Mug"` and `minPriceUsd: 18` from the original host, `extracted.product.name: "Copper Kettle Pro"` and every LD-sourced row (identifiers, structured-data evidence) from the other page. The honest answer is $18.00. Reachability, measured honestly: 2 of 397 captured stores have a page tier that lands on a different host while robots.txt does not — equator.ca redirects the product page to `equatorcoffeeroasters.com/?shpxid=…`, the store HOMEPAGE, and tinker.coffee to `www.tinkercoffee.com`. So the mechanism is captured twice and the CONSEQUENCE never is: both redirect targets carry zero Product nodes (equator.ca's has only Organization and WebSite), so the engine fell through to the .json tier and got the right product by luck. A retired-handle redirect, which lands on a real product page with complete markup, is entirely plausible in a 172-store sample, so I am not claiming this one as unreachable.
